formulas.name: Holding period return (HPR)
formulas.vars: P_0 = beginning price; P_1 = ending price; D_1 = income (dividend or coupon) received during the period
formulas.use: Total return over one holding period of any length, combining price change and income.
formulas.trap: Dropping the income term, or annualizing a multi-year HPR by dividing by years instead of compounding: (1 + HPR)^(1/N) - 1.

formulas.name: Geometric mean return
formulas.use: Compound average return per period; the right measure of past multi-period performance.
formulas.trap: Taking the root of the returns without adding 1 first; the arithmetic mean always equals or exceeds it, more so as volatility rises.

formulas.name: Harmonic mean
formulas.use: Average cost per share when an equal dollar amount is invested each period (cost averaging).
formulas.trap: Using the arithmetic mean price for equal-dollar purchases overstates cost; harmonic < geometric < arithmetic unless all values are equal.

formulas.name: Money-weighted return (MWR)
formulas.vars: CF_t = investor's net cash flow at t: contributions negative, withdrawals and ending value positive (or all reversed, consistently)
formulas.use: IRR of the investor's own cash flows; the return the investor actually earned, including the effect of timing.
formulas.trap: Ranking managers on MWR when clients control the timing of flows; large inflows just before a loss drag MWR below TWR.

formulas.name: Time-weighted return (TWR)
formulas.vars: HPR_t = return of sub-period t, split at each external cash flow; n = number of sub-periods; N = years in the measurement period
formulas.use: Manager performance standard: links sub-period returns so client contributions and withdrawals do not affect the result.
formulas.trap: Averaging sub-period returns arithmetically, or not starting a new sub-period at each external cash flow.

formulas.name: Annualized return from a periodic return
formulas.vars: c = periods per year: 4 for a quarterly return, 365/100 for a 100-day return, 1/2 for a two-year return
formulas.use: Restates a weekly, monthly, or multi-year return as a compound annual rate so different horizons can be compared.
formulas.trap: Multiplying a quarterly return by 4 or halving a two-year return; annualizing compounds, it does not scale linearly.

formulas.name: Continuously compounded return
formulas.vars: ln = natural log. A T-period r_cc is the sum of the one-period r_cc values; normal r_cc implies lognormal prices (see Simulation)
formulas.use: Converts an HPR to a log return; multi-period log returns add, which is why price simulations model them as normal.
formulas.trap: Using ln(HPR) instead of ln(1 + HPR), or treating r_cc as equal to the HPR; for any nonzero HPR, r_cc is lower.

formulas.name: Real return (Fisher relation)
formulas.vars: π = inflation over the same period; r_real ≈ r_nominal - π only as an approximation for small rates
formulas.use: Strips inflation out of a nominal return to show the change in purchasing power.
formulas.trap: Subtracting inflation when the exact real return is asked: 10% nominal with 4% inflation is 1.10/1.04 - 1 = 5.77%, not 6%.

formulas.name: Effective annual rate (EAR)
formulas.vars: r_s = stated annual rate (APR); m = compounding periods per year. Continuous compounding: EAR = e^(r_s) - 1
formulas.use: Compares loans or deposits quoted with different compounding frequencies on one annual basis.
formulas.trap: Comparing stated rates across frequencies; 12% compounded monthly is a 12.68% EAR, above 12.5% compounded annually.

formulas.name: Future value with periodic compounding
formulas.vars: r_s = stated annual rate; m = compounding periods per year; N = years. Reverse for PV: PV = FV_N / (1 + r_s/m)^(mN)
formulas.use: Grows a single lump sum forward, or discounts it back, at a stated rate with any compounding frequency.
formulas.trap: Mismatching rate and periods: quarterly compounding over 5 years uses r_s/4 for 20 periods, not r_s for 20 or r_s/4 for 5.

formulas.name: PV of an ordinary annuity and an annuity due
formulas.vars: A = level payment; r = periodic rate; N = number of payments; ordinary pays at each period end, due at each period start
formulas.use: Values a level stream of N payments such as a loan, lease, or pension; solve for A to get a loan payment.
formulas.trap: Leaving the calculator in END mode for an annuity due, or using N + 1 periods instead of multiplying by (1 + r).

formulas.name: Perpetuity: level and growing
formulas.vars: A = constant payment; CF_1 = payment one period from now; requires r > g; value is dated one period before the first payment
formulas.use: Values a payment stream with no end date, such as preferred dividends (level) or a constant-growth cash flow.
formulas.trap: Using today's payment instead of CF_1, or discounting a delayed perpetuity from its first payment date instead of one period earlier.

formulas.name: Sample variance and standard deviation
formulas.use: Measures dispersion of a sample of returns around their mean; s is in the same units as the returns.
formulas.trap: Dividing by n instead of n - 1 for a sample; only a full population variance divides by the number of observations N.

formulas.name: Target semideviation
formulas.vars: B = target return; only observations at or below B enter the sum, but n is the full sample size
formulas.use: Downside risk measure: dispersion of returns below a target such as a minimum acceptable return.
formulas.trap: Dividing by the count of below-target observations instead of n - 1, or measuring deviations from the mean rather than from B.

formulas.name: Coefficient of variation (CV)
formulas.use: Risk per unit of mean return; compares dispersion across assets with different average returns (lower is better).
formulas.trap: Using CV when the mean is near zero or negative, or confusing it with the Sharpe ratio, which uses excess return over the risk-free rate.

formulas.name: Excess kurtosis
formulas.use: Measures fat tails relative to the normal distribution, which has kurtosis 3 and excess kurtosis 0.
formulas.trap: Reading kurtosis of 3 as fat-tailed; only positive excess kurtosis (leptokurtic) means more extreme outcomes than the normal.

formulas.name: Sample covariance and correlation
formulas.use: Covariance gives the direction of co-movement; correlation scales it to the range -1 to +1 so strength can be compared.
formulas.trap: Reading a large covariance as a strong relationship without scaling by both standard deviations; zero correlation is not independence.

formulas.name: Expected value and variance from probabilities
formulas.use: Forecast mean and risk of a variable from scenario probabilities, such as EPS under recession, base, and boom cases.
formulas.trap: Averaging scenarios equally, or dividing by n - 1 as if the scenarios were a sample; the weights are the probabilities.

formulas.name: Total probability rule
formulas.vars: S_i = mutually exclusive and exhaustive scenarios whose probabilities sum to 1
formulas.use: Builds an unconditional probability from conditional ones across scenarios; it supplies the denominator in Bayes' formula.
formulas.trap: Using scenarios that overlap or miss outcomes, or adding the conditional probabilities without weighting each by P(S_i).

formulas.name: Bayes' formula
formulas.use: Updates a prior probability P(A) after new information B arrives, giving the posterior probability P(A | B).
formulas.trap: Stopping at the joint probability P(B | A)P(A) without dividing by P(B), or swapping P(A | B) with P(B | A).

formulas.name: Standardized normal variable (z)
formulas.use: Converts an outcome into standard deviations from the mean to read normal probabilities, such as shortfall risk.
formulas.trap: Using 1.65 for a 95% two-tailed band; about 90% lies within ±1.65σ, 95% within ±1.96σ, and 99% within ±2.58σ.

formulas.name: Standard error of the sample mean
formulas.vars: Use σ/√n when the population standard deviation σ is known
formulas.use: Measures how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean; input to confidence intervals and t-tests.
formulas.trap: Confusing the standard deviation of returns with the standard error of the mean; quadrupling n only halves the standard error.

formulas.name: Confidence interval for the population mean
formulas.vars: z: 1.65 (90%), 1.96 (95%), 2.58 (99%). t has n - 1 df and is the right choice when σ is unknown; for large n, z is an acceptable approximation
formulas.use: Range likely to contain the true mean at confidence 1 - α; wider for higher confidence or smaller samples.
formulas.trap: Saying there is a 95% probability the true mean is in this interval; 95% of intervals built this way would contain it.

formulas.name: Test statistic for a population mean
formulas.vars: μ_0 = hypothesized mean; df = n - 1; use z with σ in place of s when the population variance is known
formulas.use: Tests whether a sample mean differs from a hypothesized value; reject H0 when |t| exceeds the critical value.
formulas.trap: Dividing by s instead of s/√n, which uses the dispersion of single returns rather than the standard error of the mean.

formulas.name: t-test of a correlation coefficient
formulas.use: Tests H0: population correlation = 0 with n - 2 degrees of freedom; significance depends on both r and n.
formulas.trap: Using n - 1 degrees of freedom, or reading a significant correlation as evidence that one variable causes the other.

formulas.name: Spearman rank correlation
formulas.vars: d_i = difference between the two ranks of observation i; for large samples (n > 30) test H0: ρ_S = 0 with the correlation t-test, n - 2 df
formulas.use: Nonparametric correlation of ranks; use it when data are ranked, non-normal, or have outliers that distort the Pearson r.
formulas.trap: Using differences in raw values instead of ranks for d_i, or dividing by n² instead of n(n² - 1).

formulas.name: Chi-square test of independence
formulas.vars: O_ij = observed count; E_ij = (row i total × column j total) / grand total; r, c = rows and columns of the table
formulas.use: Nonparametric test of whether two categorical classifications in a contingency table are independent.
formulas.trap: Using n - 1 degrees of freedom, or setting expected counts to an equal share of the total instead of row × column / total.

formulas.name: OLS slope and intercept
formulas.vars: Prediction: Ŷ = b̂_0 + b̂_1 X; the fitted line passes through the point of means (X̄, Ȳ)
formulas.use: Estimates the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals; the slope is the change in Y per unit change in X.
formulas.trap: Dividing the covariance by Var(Y) instead of Var(X), or forecasting with an X far outside the range used to fit the line.

formulas.name: Coefficient of determination (R²)
formulas.vars: SST = total variation of Y; SSR = variation explained by the regression; SSE = unexplained (residual); SST = SSR + SSE
formulas.use: Share of the variation in Y explained by X; in simple regression R² equals the squared correlation of X and Y.
formulas.trap: Reading a high R² as proof of causation, or forgetting that r = ±√R² takes the sign of the slope.

formulas.name: F-statistic for the regression
formulas.vars: df = 1 and n - 2 in simple regression; F equals the square of the slope's t-statistic
formulas.use: Tests H0: slope = 0 as a one-tailed test of explained versus unexplained variation per degree of freedom.
formulas.trap: Dividing SSE by n instead of n - 2, or inverting the ratio so the unexplained mean square sits in the numerator.

formulas.name: Standard error of the estimate (SEE)
formulas.use: Typical size of a prediction error around the regression line; a lower SEE means a tighter fit.
formulas.trap: Dividing SSE by n or n - 1; simple regression loses two degrees of freedom because it estimates a slope and an intercept.

definitions.def: Gross return is measured after trading costs but before management and administrative fees; net return deducts those fees. Gross return judges manager skill; net return is what the investor kept.
Simple average of periodic returns and the best estimate of a single future period's expected return. It always equals or exceeds the geometric mean, so it overstates multi-period compound growth.
Asymmetry of a distribution. Positive skew has a long right tail (mean > median > mode); negative skew has a long left tail of large losses (mean < median < mode) that standard deviation understates.
Mutually exclusive events cannot both occur, so P(A and B) = 0. Independent events can occur together; one does not change the other's probability, so P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).
Joint probability P(AB) is the chance both events occur; conditional probability P(A | B) = P(AB) / P(B) is the chance of A given that B occurred. Multiplying P(A | B) by P(B) recovers the joint.

If continuously compounded returns are normal, prices are lognormal: bounded below by zero and right-skewed. A normal distribution fits log returns, not prices, because it would allow negative prices.
For large samples (n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal with mean μ and variance σ²/n, whatever the population's shape. It does not make individual returns normal.

Monte Carlo draws inputs from assumed probability distributions; bootstrapping resamples observed history with replacement. Bootstrapping needs no distribution assumption but cannot create patterns absent from the data.

definitions.term: Type I and Type II errors
definitions.def: Type I: rejecting a true null hypothesis, with probability α (the significance level). Type II: failing to reject a false null, with probability β. Lowering α raises β unless the sample grows.
Power = 1 - β, the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. It rises with sample size and with α, so a stricter significance level lowers power.
The smallest significance level at which the null hypothesis can be rejected; reject when p < α. It is not the probability that the null is true and says nothing about effect size.

Parametric tests concern parameters such as a mean and rely on distribution assumptions. Nonparametric tests, such as chi-square or Spearman rank correlation, suit ranked or categorical data and non-normal samples.

A linear relationship between X and Y, and residuals that have constant variance (homoskedasticity), are independent of each other, and are normally distributed. Violations make standard errors and tests unreliable.

distractors: Annualized return from a periodic return
drill.why: The T-th root of the product of (1 + R_t) over T equal periods is the compound average return per period. TWR uses the same product but takes the root over years N and splits at cash flows; the harmonic mean averages reciprocals.

distractors: Annualized return from a periodic return
drill.why: A stated annual rate divided by m and compounded m times is the effective annual rate. Annualizing compounds an observed periodic return, not a quoted rate split by m; future value multiplies a PV over mN periods.
The natural log of the price relative is the continuously compounded return, which adds across periods. The HPR is the price relative minus 1 with no log; continuous EAR runs the other way, e^r - 1.

One minus six times the summed squared rank differences over n(n² - 1) is the Spearman rank correlation. The correlation t-test uses r and n - 2 to test significance; the Pearson r divides covariance by both standard deviations.

distractors: Standard error of the sample mean
drill.why: Only observations at or below the target B enter the sum, so the result measures downside dispersion. Sample standard deviation squares deviations from the mean for every observation; the standard error divides s by √n.

distractors: Test statistic for a population mean
drill.why: Dividing the sample standard deviation by √n gives the dispersion of the sample mean, its standard error. CV divides s by the mean, not by √n; the t-statistic divides a mean difference by this standard error.

distractors: Test statistic for a population mean
drill.why: A sample correlation r times √(n - 2) over √(1 - r²) is the t-statistic for H0: ρ = 0 with n - 2 df. Spearman's r_S is a correlation itself, not a test statistic; the test of a mean uses (X̄ - μ0)/(s/√n).

distractors: Expected value and variance from probabilities
drill.why: The likelihood P(B | A) times the prior P(A), divided by P(B), is the updated posterior P(A | B). The total probability rule sums P(A | S_i)P(S_i) across scenarios and supplies the denominator, not the posterior.
Explained variation over total variation is R², the share of the variation in Y explained by X. The F-statistic also uses SSR but divides mean squares, MSR/MSE; SEE is the square root of SSE/(n - 2).
Explained over unexplained variation, each divided by its degrees of freedom, is the F-statistic. R² divides SSR by SST with no degrees-of-freedom adjustment; SEE is the square root of MSE alone.

formulas.name: Own-price elasticity of demand
formulas.use: Measures how quantity demanded responds to the good's own price; if |E_P| > 1 demand is elastic and a price cut raises revenue.
formulas.trap: Judging elasticity by its sign instead of |E_P|, or assuming a price cut always lifts revenue; with inelastic demand revenue falls.

formulas.name: Cross-price and income elasticity
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} E_{XY} = \frac{\%\Delta Q_X}{\%\Delta P_Y} \\ E_I = \frac{\%\Delta Q_d}{\%\Delta I} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: P_Y = price of another good; I = consumer income. E_XY > 0 substitutes, < 0 complements; E_I > 0 normal good, < 0 inferior good
formulas.use: Classifies goods: cross elasticity separates substitutes from complements, income elasticity separates normal from inferior goods.
formulas.trap: Reading the sign backwards: negative cross elasticity means complements, and negative income elasticity means an inferior good.

formulas.name: Profit-maximizing output and monopoly price
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} MR = MC \text{ (every market structure)} \\ \text{Monopoly: } P > MR = MC \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Finds the profit-maximizing output; a monopolist then charges the highest price that demand allows at that output.
formulas.trap: Setting a monopolist's output where P = MC, or assuming it charges the highest possible price regardless of demand.

formulas.name: Perfect competition long-run equilibrium
formulas.use: Price-taking firms enter until price falls to minimum average total cost, leaving zero economic profit in the long run.
formulas.trap: Confusing zero economic profit with zero accounting profit; firms still earn a normal return that covers the cost of capital.

formulas.name: Monopolistic competition long-run equilibrium
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} MR = MC \\ P = ATC > \min ATC \text{ (long run)} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Entry erodes economic profit to zero, but differentiated firms produce less than the minimum-ATC output (excess capacity).
formulas.trap: Expecting lasting economic profit as in monopoly, or production at minimum ATC as in perfect competition.

formulas.name: Breakeven and shutdown rules
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Short run: operate if } P \ge AVC \\ \text{Long run: exit if } P < ATC \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: AVC = average variable cost; ATC = average total cost; breakeven is P = ATC (zero economic profit)
formulas.use: Decides whether a loss-making firm keeps producing: fixed costs are sunk in the short run, so price only needs to cover AVC.
formulas.trap: Shutting down as soon as price falls below ATC; in the short run any price above AVC still contributes to fixed costs.

formulas.name: Concentration ratio and HHI
formulas.vars: s_i = market share of firm i; CR_N sums the N largest firms; HHI sums squared shares of all M firms (in percent, maximum 10,000)
formulas.use: Gauges market power; HHI weights large firms more, so it registers mergers among the leaders that CR_N can miss.
formulas.trap: Relying on CR_N: if two top-4 firms merge, CR_4 rises only by the fifth firm's share while HHI jumps. Also mixing decimal and percent shares.

formulas.name: Unemployment rate
formulas.vars: Labor force = employed + unemployed people actively seeking work; discouraged workers are outside the labor force
formulas.use: Lagging gauge of labor-market slack; compare it with the natural rate (frictional + structural) to place the cycle.
formulas.trap: Dividing by the working-age population, or counting discouraged workers as unemployed; when they stop searching the rate falls.

formulas.name: Fiscal multiplier
formulas.vars: c = marginal propensity to consume (MPC); t = tax rate
formulas.use: Change in GDP per $1 of extra government spending; MPC 0.80 and a 25% tax rate give 1 / 0.40 = 2.5.
formulas.trap: Using 1/(1 - MPC) and ignoring taxes, or applying the spending multiplier to an equal tax cut, which has a smaller effect.

formulas.name: Money multiplier
formulas.use: Maximum new money created per $1 of new reserves in a fractional-reserve system; a 10% requirement gives a multiplier of 10.
formulas.trap: Treating it as exact; excess reserves held by banks and cash held by the public make actual money creation smaller.

formulas.name: Quantity theory of money
formulas.vars: M = money supply; V = velocity of money; P = price level; Y = real output; PY = nominal GDP
formulas.use: Links money growth to inflation: with V and Y stable, the percentage change in M passes through to P.
formulas.trap: Assuming money growth always raises inflation one-for-one; that needs constant velocity and output (long-run money neutrality).

formulas.name: Neutral policy rate
formulas.use: Policy rate that neither stimulates nor restrains; a policy rate below neutral is expansionary, above it contractionary.
formulas.trap: Judging the stance by whether rates look high in absolute terms rather than relative to neutral, which is estimated, not observed.

formulas.name: Current account and national saving
formulas.vars: S = private saving; I = investment; T - G = government budget balance; CA is approximately exports minus imports (X - M)
formulas.use: A current account deficit means domestic saving falls short of investment plus any budget deficit, so foreign capital fills the gap.
formulas.trap: Dropping the government term, or treating a deficit as always bad; it can finance productive domestic investment.

formulas.name: Cross exchange rate
formulas.vars: Price/base notation: JPY/EUR = yen per 1 euro (the base currency is the one that equals 1 unit)
formulas.use: Derives the rate between two currencies from their quotes against a common currency such as the US dollar.
formulas.trap: Multiplying quotes whose common currency does not cancel; invert one first (EUR/USD = 1 / USD/EUR) so the dollars divide out.

formulas.name: Forward rate from forward points
formulas.vars: 10,000 fits a 4-decimal quote. Points are in units of the quote's last decimal, so divide by 100 for a 2-decimal quote such as JPY/USD
formulas.use: Converts a dealer's forward points into an outright forward rate; positive points mean the base currency trades at a premium.
formulas.trap: Adding points as whole numbers or percentages; +25 points on a 1.0800 spot gives a 1.0825 forward.

formulas.name: Forward premium or discount
formulas.vars: Price/base quotes; i_P, i_B = annual interest rates; τ = actual days / 360; a positive result is a forward premium on the base currency
formulas.use: Size of the forward premium or discount on the base currency implied by the interest-rate differential under covered parity.
formulas.trap: Expecting the higher-yield currency to trade at a premium; the base currency is at a forward premium only when i_B is below i_P.

formulas.name: Covered interest rate parity forward rate
formulas.vars: i_P, i_B = annual money-market rates of the price and base currencies; τ = actual days / 360, the curriculum's convention (some markets use 365)
formulas.use: No-arbitrage forward rate: a covered investment earns the same in either currency; a different market forward means arbitrage.
formulas.trap: Putting the base-currency rate in the numerator, or using full annual rates for a 6-month forward without scaling by τ.

formulas.name: Real exchange rate
formulas.vars: S_P/B = nominal spot rate (price currency per unit of base); CPI_B, CPI_P = price levels in the base and price-currency countries
formulas.use: Purchasing-power version of the exchange rate; a rise means the base currency has appreciated in real terms.
formulas.trap: Inverting the price ratio; a higher base-country price level raises the base currency's real value even at an unchanged spot rate.

formulas.name: Percentage change in a currency
formulas.vars: S_0, S_1 = old and new spot quotes in price/base notation
formulas.use: Measures appreciation or depreciation of each currency in a quote; the two changes are not equal and opposite.
formulas.trap: Assuming both currencies moved by the same percentage: USD/EUR from 1.10 to 1.21 is euro +10% but dollar -9.09%.

formulas.name: Marshall-Lerner condition
formulas.vars: ω_X, ω_M = exports and imports as shares of total trade; ε_X, ε_M = price elasticities of export and import demand (absolute values)
formulas.use: Condition under which a currency depreciation improves the trade balance: export and import demand must be elastic enough.
formulas.trap: Expecting an immediate improvement; trade volumes adjust slowly, so the balance usually worsens first (the J-curve).

definitions.def: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs from revenue; economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs, including a normal return on capital. Zero economic profit still means a normal accounting return.

Demand for a normal good rises with income (income elasticity > 0); demand for an inferior good falls as income rises (income elasticity < 0). Luxuries are normal goods with income elasticity above 1.
Substitutes have positive cross-price elasticity: a higher price for one raises demand for the other. Complements have negative cross-price elasticity because they are consumed together.

A few interdependent firms behind high entry barriers. Models: kinked demand (rivals match price cuts, not increases), Cournot, Stackelberg, dominant firm. Cartels are unstable because each member gains by cheating.
Recovery: output below trend but rising. Expansion: above trend and rising. Slowdown: above trend but growth slowing. Contraction: below trend and falling. Phases vary in length and depth.

Leading indicators (building permits, yield-curve spread, new orders) turn before the economy; coincident ones (payrolls, industrial production) move with it; lagging ones (unemployment duration) confirm turns.

Frictional: workers between jobs. Structural: skills or location no longer match the jobs available. Cyclical: caused by weak demand in a downturn. The natural rate includes frictional and structural, so it is above 0%.

Cost-push inflation comes from higher input costs that cut aggregate supply, so prices rise as output falls. Demand-pull inflation comes from demand growing faster than capacity. Core inflation excludes food and energy.

definitions.term: Fiscal policy lags and automatic stabilizers
definitions.def: Discretionary fiscal policy faces recognition, action, and impact lags, so stimulus can arrive late. Automatic stabilizers such as progressive taxes and unemployment benefits respond without new legislation.
When demand for money is highly elastic near the effective lower bound, extra reserves do not lower rates or raise spending, so central banks turn to quantitative easing and forward guidance.

Easy fiscal with tight monetary policy brings high real rates, crowded-out private investment, and a larger public sector share. Tight fiscal with easy monetary policy brings low rates and a larger private sector share.

Cooperation vs non-cooperation crossed with globalization vs nationalism: multilateralism (cooperative, global), bilateralism (cooperative, national), hegemony (uncooperative, global), autarky (uncooperative, national).

Event risk follows a known calendar (elections, legislation); exogenous risk is a sudden shock (an invasion); thematic risk is a long-running trend (cyber threats). Assess each by likelihood, velocity, and impact.

Absolute advantage means producing more with the same inputs; comparative advantage means a lower opportunity cost. Trade gains come from comparative advantage, so even the less productive country gains.

Both raise the domestic price, help domestic producers, and hurt consumers, with a deadweight loss. A tariff gives revenue to the government; quota rents go to license holders or exporters unless licenses are auctioned.
After a depreciation, import prices rise at once while trade volumes adjust slowly, so the trade balance worsens before it improves, provided the Marshall-Lerner condition holds.

drill.why: The percentage change in a good's own quantity demanded over the percentage change in its own price is own-price elasticity. Cross elasticity divides by another good's price change, and income elasticity by the change in income.

One over one minus the after-tax marginal propensity to consume, c(1 - t), is the fiscal multiplier on government spending. The money multiplier is also one over a fraction, but the fraction is the reserve requirement.

One divided by the reserve requirement is the maximum deposits created per unit of new reserves, the money multiplier. The fiscal multiplier has the same 1-over shape but divides by 1 - c(1 - t), with consumption and tax terms.

Private saving minus investment plus the government balance equals the current account: national saving not used at home is lent abroad. The Marshall-Lerner condition is about trade elasticities, not saving and investment.

Spot times the ratio of price-currency to base-currency interest growth is the covered-parity forward rate. The forward premium uses the same rates but gives (F - S)/S; the real exchange rate scales spot by price levels, not interest rates.

distractors: Covered interest rate parity forward rate
drill.why: Scaling the nominal spot rate by base-country over price-country price levels gives the real exchange rate. Covered parity scales spot by interest-rate factors; a cross rate multiplies two nominal quotes so a common currency cancels.

distractors: Covered interest rate parity forward rate
drill.why: The interest differential scaled by τ and divided by the base-currency growth factor equals (F - S)/S, the forward premium on the base currency. Covered parity gives the forward level itself; a percentage change compares two spot rates.

formulas.name: Votes needed to elect one director (cumulative)
formulas.vars: Total votes = shares voting x seats up for election; to win k seats a holder needs more than k x Total votes / (Seats up + 1)
formulas.use: Tests whether a minority holder can win a board seat by concentrating all cumulative votes on one candidate.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to multiply shares by seats to get total votes, or dividing by the number of seats instead of seats + 1.

formulas.name: Cost of trade credit (forgone discount)
formulas.vars: d = discount as a decimal (0.02 for 2/10 net 30); N = net days; D = discount days, so N - D is the extra days of financing
formulas.use: Annual cost of skipping an early-payment discount; take the discount when this beats the firm's short-term borrowing rate.
formulas.trap: Using d instead of d/(1 - d), or 365/N instead of 365/(N - D): the financing period is only the days beyond the discount window.

formulas.name: Effective cost of short-term borrowing
formulas.vars: Fees = commitment fee, dealer commission, backup-line cost; net proceeds = cash received; m = periods per year (12 for one month), a simple annualization
formulas.use: Compares a credit line, banker's acceptance and commercial paper on one annualized basis to pick the cheapest short-term source.
formulas.trap: Dividing by face value for discount instruments: commercial paper and banker's acceptances deliver face minus interest, so cost is higher.

formulas.name: Net present value (NPV) decision rule
formulas.vars: CF_0 = initial outlay (negative); r = required return for the project's risk, not the firm's cost of debt
formulas.use: Accept independent projects with NPV > 0; among mutually exclusive projects take the highest NPV, even if its IRR is lower.
formulas.trap: Discounting a riskier-than-average project at the firm's WACC, or putting sunk costs or interest payments into CF_t instead of the rate.

formulas.name: Internal rate of return (IRR) decision rule
formulas.use: Discount rate that sets NPV to zero; accept a conventional independent project when IRR exceeds the required return r.
formulas.trap: Ranking mutually exclusive projects by IRR; it ignores scale, assumes reinvestment at the IRR, and nonconventional flows give multiple IRRs.

formulas.name: Profitability index (PI)
formulas.vars: I_0 = initial investment, entered as a positive amount
formulas.use: Ranks divisible projects under capital rationing by value per dollar invested; PI > 1 is the same signal as NPV > 0.
formulas.trap: Subtracting the initial outlay in the numerator, which gives NPV/I_0 and moves the accept threshold from 1 to 0.

formulas.name: Return on invested capital (ROIC)
formulas.vars: NOPAT = EBIT x (1 - t); invested capital = debt + equity funding the operating business
formulas.use: Judges past capital allocation: ROIC above the cost of capital creates value, below it destroys value even with positive profit.
formulas.trap: Comparing ROIC with the cost of debt instead of the cost of capital (WACC), or treating positive earnings as value creation.

formulas.name: Project value with real options
formulas.use: Values flexibility a static NPV misses (timing, abandonment, expansion); a small negative-NPV project can still be worth taking.
formulas.trap: Adding option value that the cash flow forecast already reflects, which double-counts the flexibility.

formulas.name: After-tax cost of debt
formulas.vars: r_d = current market YTM on the firm's debt (matrix-priced yield for similar rating and maturity if untraded); t = marginal tax rate
formulas.use: Converts the market yield on new debt into the after-tax rate that enters WACC when interest is tax-deductible.
formulas.trap: Using the coupon rate instead of the current YTM, or applying (1 - t) when the firm cannot use the interest deduction.

formulas.name: Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
formulas.vars: w = target market-value weights summing to 1; r_e usually from CAPM (Portfolio Management); add w_p r_p if preferred stock is outstanding
formulas.use: Hurdle rate for average-risk projects and the discount rate for cash flows available to all capital providers.
formulas.trap: Using book-value weights, or applying (1 - t) to the cost of equity instead of only to the cost of debt.

formulas.name: MM Proposition I with taxes
formulas.vars: tD = PV of the interest tax shield on permanent debt D; without taxes V_L = V_U, so capital structure is irrelevant
formulas.use: Shows that with corporate taxes and no distress costs, debt adds value equal to the tax rate times the amount of debt.
formulas.trap: Concluding firms should be 100% debt-financed; the static trade-off theory adds distress costs that cap optimal leverage.

formulas.name: MM Proposition II: cost of equity and leverage
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} r_e = r_0 + (r_0 - r_d)\frac{D}{E} \\ r_e = r_0 + (r_0 - r_d)(1 - t)\frac{D}{E} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Line 1: no taxes; line 2: with taxes. r_0 = cost of capital of the all-equity firm; r_d = pre-tax cost of debt
formulas.use: Cost of equity rises linearly with D/E as equity gets riskier; with no taxes WACC stays at r_0 whatever the leverage.
formulas.trap: Dropping (1 - t) in the with-taxes version, or using D/V instead of D/E as the leverage term.

formulas.name: ROE with financial leverage
formulas.vars: ROA = EBIT / total assets; r_d = interest rate on debt; ignores taxes (multiply the result by 1 - t for after-tax ROE)
formulas.use: Shows how debt magnifies ROE: leverage raises ROE only while the return on assets exceeds the cost of debt.
formulas.trap: Assuming leverage always raises ROE; once ROA falls below r_d, every extra unit of D/E lowers ROE.

formulas.name: Customer lifetime value (simple LTV)
formulas.latex: LTV = \frac{\text{Margin per period}}{\text{Churn rate per period}}
formulas.use: Estimates value per subscriber for unit economics; compare LTV with customer acquisition cost (CAC) before funding growth.
formulas.trap: Mixing a monthly margin with an annual churn rate, or using revenue instead of contribution margin per customer.

definitions.def: A business with at least one general partner who manages it and has unlimited liability, plus limited partners whose liability is capped at their investment and who do not manage it.
A legal entity separate from its owners: shareholders have limited liability and can transfer shares easily, but profits can be taxed twice, at the company level and again as dividends.
Listing existing shares on an exchange without underwriters and without raising new capital; an IPO, by contrast, sells new shares through underwriters to raise funds.

definitions.term: Equity as a call option on firm assets
definitions.def: With limited liability, shareholders keep all upside above the debt claim and lose at most their investment, so near distress they gain from risk-taking that creditors bear.
The view that the board should balance the interests of shareholders, creditors, employees, customers, suppliers and communities, unlike shareholder theory, which puts shareholder value first.
Managers (agents) acting in their own interest rather than shareholders' (principals'), through perks, empire-building acquisitions, entrenchment or too little risk-taking.
Each share gets one vote per seat up for election and votes can be pooled on one candidate, letting minority holders win seats; straight voting gives the majority every seat.
Primary sources are cash, short-term investments, operating cash flow, trade credit and bank lines; secondary sources (asset sales, debt renegotiation, bankruptcy) change operations or finances.
A drag delays cash inflows (slow-paying customers, obsolete inventory); a pull speeds up cash outflows (suppliers shortening credit terms, earlier payments).
A conservative approach funds working capital with long-term capital, costing more but cutting rollover risk; an aggressive approach uses cheaper short-term funding with more refinancing risk.
Money already spent that cannot be recovered; it is irrelevant to a project decision, unlike opportunity costs, which are incremental and must be included.
Firms add debt until the marginal value of the interest tax shield equals the marginal expected cost of financial distress, which defines an optimal target capital structure.
Because of information asymmetry, managers prefer internal funds, then debt, then new equity last; it predicts no target debt ratio, and an equity issue signals overvaluation.
A product becomes more valuable as more users join, as on platforms linking buyers and sellers; this can create winner-take-most markets, but multi-homing users weaken the effect.

drill.why: The rate that makes the discounted cash flows sum to zero is the IRR. NPV uses the same sum but discounts at a given required return r and reports dollars; PI divides the PV of future flows by the outlay.

Starting from the unlevered cost of capital r_0 and adding the after-tax spread over r_d times D/E gives the levered cost of equity, MM II with taxes. ROE with leverage has the same shape but starts from ROA, an accounting return.

distractors: MM Proposition II: cost of equity and leverage
drill.why: Unlevered firm value plus the debt tax shield tD is levered firm value, MM Proposition I with taxes. Real options also add to a base value, but to project NPV; MM II gives the cost of equity, not value.

distractors: MM Proposition II: cost of equity and leverage
drill.why: Return on assets plus its spread over the cost of debt, scaled by D/E, is accounting ROE under leverage. MM II has the same shape but starts from r_0 and gives the required return on equity.

The discount over the net amount paid, compounded over the extra days of credit, is the annual cost of forgoing a supplier discount. Short-term borrowing cost divides interest plus fees by net proceeds.
PV of future cash flows per dollar of initial outlay is the profitability index; above 1 means NPV > 0. NPV is a dollar sum, not a ratio, and ROIC is an accounting return on capital already invested.

formulas.name: Revenue recognized over time (cost-to-cost)
formulas.vars: Price = total contract price; prior cum. revenue = revenue already recognized on the contract in earlier periods
formulas.use: Computes this period's revenue on a long-term contract satisfied over time, measuring progress by cost incurred.
formulas.trap: Reporting cumulative revenue as this period's revenue; subtract what was already recognized. An expected loss is booked in full at once.

formulas.name: Basic and diluted EPS
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Basic EPS} = \frac{NI - PD}{WASO} \\ \text{Diluted EPS} = \frac{NI - PD + PD_{conv} + Int_{conv}(1-t)}{WASO + \text{Conv. shares} + \text{TSM shares}} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: PD = preferred dividends; PD_conv = dividends on convertible preferred; Int_conv = interest on convertible debt; WASO = weighted average common shares
formulas.use: Basic EPS uses actual shares; diluted EPS adds dilutive convertibles (if-converted method) and options (treasury stock method).
formulas.trap: Including an antidilutive security; test each one and drop any that raises EPS. Convertible-debt interest is added back after tax.

formulas.name: Treasury stock method incremental shares
formulas.vars: n = shares issued if options or warrants are exercised; X = exercise price; P-bar = average market price for the period
formulas.use: Adds the net new shares from in-the-money options or warrants to the diluted EPS denominator, assuming proceeds buy back stock.
formulas.trap: Using the year-end price instead of the average price, or including options with X above the average price; those are antidilutive.

formulas.name: Comprehensive income
formulas.use: Totals all non-owner changes in equity, adding OCI items such as translation adjustments and pension remeasurements to net income.
formulas.trap: Thinking dividends paid or shares issued pass through comprehensive income; transactions with owners bypass it entirely.

formulas.name: Operating cash flow, indirect method
formulas.vars: Gains and losses = non-operating items such as asset sales, whose proceeds belong in investing cash flow
formulas.use: Reconciles net income to cash from operations; the method most firms report and the usual exam calculation.
formulas.trap: Reversing the working-capital signs: a rise in receivables or inventory reduces CFO, and a rise in payables increases it.

formulas.name: Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF)
formulas.vars: Int = interest expense; t = tax rate; FCInv = capital expenditures net of proceeds from long-term asset sales
formulas.use: Measures cash available to all capital providers after reinvestment; start from CFO when a cash flow statement is given.
formulas.trap: Adding back pre-tax interest, or adding interest an IFRS firm already classified as financing, so it never reduced CFO.

formulas.name: Free cash flow to equity (FCFE)
formulas.vars: Net borrowing = new debt issued minus debt repaid
formulas.use: Measures cash available to common shareholders after reinvestment and after all debt flows.
formulas.trap: Adding back after-tax interest as in FCFF; interest belongs to lenders, so FCFE starts from CFO with no interest add-back.

formulas.name: Cash flow interest coverage
formulas.use: Measures how many times operating cash before interest and taxes covers cash interest; a cash check on EBIT coverage.
formulas.trap: Using CFO alone as the numerator; interest and taxes paid were deducted to reach CFO and must be added back first.

formulas.name: Reinvestment and debt coverage ratios
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Reinvestment} = \frac{CFO}{\text{Cash paid for long-term assets}} \\ \text{Debt coverage} = \frac{CFO}{\text{Total debt}} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Show whether operating cash can fund capital spending internally and how much of total debt one year of CFO would repay.
formulas.trap: Using net income or EBITDA instead of CFO; both are cash ratios, and total debt includes current borrowings.

formulas.name: Cash flow to net income and aggregate accruals
formulas.vars: Warning sign: CFO/NI persistently below 1 or falling; aggregate accruals = the part of reported earnings not yet backed by operating cash
formulas.use: Flags earnings quality: when net income consistently outruns operating cash flow, earnings rest on accruals that may later reverse.
formulas.trap: Reading NI above CFO as strength; large or rising accruals often precede write-downs, and CFO lifted by stretching payables is not quality.

formulas.name: Inventory and COGS identity
formulas.vars: BI = beginning inventory; EI = ending inventory
formulas.use: Links the balance sheet and income statement; solve for purchases (for payables turnover) or for a missing inventory figure.
formulas.trap: Treating COGS as cash paid to suppliers; purchases = COGS + increase in inventory, then adjust for the change in payables.

formulas.name: LIFO to FIFO: inventory and equity
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} Inv_{FIFO} = Inv_{LIFO} + LR_{end} \\ Equity_{FIFO} = Equity_{LIFO} + LR_{end}(1-t) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: LR_end = ending LIFO reserve disclosed by the US GAAP LIFO firm; t = tax rate
formulas.use: Restates a LIFO firm's balance sheet to FIFO so inventory, current ratio and leverage compare with IFRS or FIFO peers.
formulas.trap: Adding the full reserve to equity; only LR(1 - t) goes to equity, and LR x t is added to deferred tax liabilities.

formulas.name: LIFO to FIFO: COGS and net income
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} COGS_{FIFO} = COGS_{LIFO} - \Delta LR \\ NI_{FIFO} = NI_{LIFO} + \Delta LR(1-t) \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Delta LR = ending minus beginning LIFO reserve; a falling reserve raises FIFO COGS
formulas.use: Restates a LIFO firm's COGS, margins and net income to FIFO for comparison with IFRS or FIFO peers.
formulas.trap: Subtracting the ending reserve from COGS; the income statement uses only the change in the reserve, the balance sheet the ending one.

formulas.name: Goodwill in an acquisition
formulas.use: Measures goodwill recognized when one company acquires another; it is tested for impairment at least annually.
formulas.trap: Subtracting book value instead of fair value of net assets, or amortizing goodwill; impairments are also never reversed.

formulas.name: Straight-line and units-of-production depreciation
formulas.use: Straight-line spreads the depreciable base evenly; units of production ties each year's expense to actual output.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to subtract salvage value; both methods depreciate cost minus salvage, unlike double-declining balance.

formulas.name: Double-declining balance depreciation
formulas.use: Applies twice the straight-line rate to opening book value, front-loading expense and lowering early-year profit and assets.
formulas.trap: Subtracting salvage before applying the rate; DDB ignores salvage until book value reaches it, then depreciation stops.

formulas.name: Average age and remaining life of PP&E
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Average age} = \frac{\text{Accumulated depreciation}}{\text{Depreciation expense}} \\ \text{Remaining life} = \frac{\text{Net PP\&E}}{\text{Depreciation expense}} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: Assumes straight-line depreciation; total useful life = gross PP&E / depreciation expense
formulas.use: Estimate in years how old the asset base is and how soon major replacement capex is due, versus peers.
formulas.trap: Using gross PP&E for remaining life; net PP&E (gross minus accumulated depreciation) over depreciation gives years left.

formulas.name: Lease liability (present value of payments)
formulas.vars: PMT = lease payment at period end; r = rate implicit in the lease or lessee's incremental borrowing rate; N = lease term
formulas.use: Measures the initial lease liability and right-of-use asset a lessee records; the liability then accrues interest at r.
formulas.trap: Expensing the payment as rent under IFRS 16; expense is depreciation plus interest, which exceeds the cash paid early on.

formulas.name: Funded status of a pension plan
formulas.vars: PBO = projected benefit obligation (IFRS: defined benefit obligation)
formulas.use: Shows whether a defined benefit plan is over- or underfunded; a negative result is reported as a net pension liability.
formulas.trap: Reversing the sign, or forgetting that a lower discount rate raises the PBO and widens a deficit with assets unchanged.

formulas.name: Deferred tax liability
formulas.vars: For an asset; t = enacted tax rate expected to apply when the difference reverses
formulas.use: Measures the future tax owed when an asset's carrying amount exceeds its tax base, as with accelerated tax depreciation.
formulas.trap: Getting the direction wrong: an asset whose tax base exceeds its carrying amount, or a liability carried above its tax base, gives a DTA.

formulas.name: Income tax expense and effective tax rate
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Tax expense} = \text{Taxes payable} + \Delta DTL - \Delta DTA \\ \text{ETR} = \frac{\text{Income tax expense}}{\text{Pre-tax income}} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Reconciles reported tax expense with taxes owed, then tests whether a low or volatile effective rate is sustainable.
formulas.trap: Dividing taxes payable by pre-tax income; the effective rate uses income tax expense, which includes deferred taxes.

formulas.name: Current and quick ratios
formulas.vars: MS = short-term marketable securities
formulas.use: Measure ability to meet short-term obligations; the quick ratio drops inventory and prepaids, which convert to cash slowly.
formulas.trap: Including inventory or prepaid expenses in the quick ratio; a wide gap to the current ratio signals reliance on inventory.

formulas.name: Cash ratio and defensive interval
formulas.vars: Daily cash expenditures = cash operating expenses / 365, excluding non-cash charges such as depreciation
formulas.use: The cash ratio is the strictest liquidity test; the defensive interval counts days of expenses payable with no new inflows.
formulas.trap: Dividing the defensive interval by current liabilities; its denominator is daily cash expenditures, so the result is days.

formulas.name: Receivables turnover and DSO
formulas.vars: DSO = days of sales outstanding; credit sales are the ideal numerator when disclosed
formulas.use: Measures how fast customers pay; DSO rising faster than peers can signal loose credit or aggressive revenue recognition.
formulas.trap: Inverting the ratio or mixing 360 and 365 days; a higher turnover and a lower DSO both mean faster collection.

formulas.name: Inventory turnover and DOH
formulas.vars: DOH = days of inventory on hand
formulas.use: Measures how many times inventory is sold and replaced each year and how many days of supply the firm holds.
formulas.trap: Using revenue instead of COGS as the numerator; inventory is carried at cost, so revenue overstates turnover.

formulas.name: Payables turnover and DPO
formulas.vars: Purchases = COGS + ending inventory - beginning inventory; DPO = days of payables outstanding
formulas.use: Measures how long the firm takes to pay suppliers; a rising DPO frees cash but can also signal liquidity stress.
formulas.trap: Using revenue as the numerator; payables arise from purchases at cost, and COGS is only a proxy when inventory is stable.

formulas.name: Cash conversion cycle
formulas.use: Measures days between paying suppliers and collecting from customers; a shorter cycle needs less working capital financing.
formulas.trap: Adding DPO instead of subtracting it; a negative cycle, common at large retailers, is usually a strength, not a red flag.

formulas.name: Total and fixed asset turnover
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Total asset turnover} = \frac{\text{Revenue}}{\text{Avg total assets}} \\ \text{Fixed asset turnover} = \frac{\text{Revenue}}{\text{Avg net fixed assets}} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Measure revenue generated per dollar of assets; total asset turnover is the efficiency term in DuPont ROE.
formulas.trap: Reading a high fixed asset turnover as pure efficiency; an old, heavily depreciated asset base inflates it.

formulas.name: Debt-to-equity and debt-to-capital
formulas.vars: Total debt = interest-bearing short- and long-term borrowings, usually including lease liabilities
formulas.use: Measure reliance on borrowed capital; debt-to-capital stays between 0 and 1, which eases comparison across firms.
formulas.trap: Counting accounts payable and other non-interest-bearing liabilities as debt, or leaving lease liabilities out.

formulas.name: Debt-to-assets and financial leverage
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Debt-to-assets} = \frac{\text{Total debt}}{\text{Total assets}} \\ \text{Financial leverage} = \frac{\text{Avg total assets}}{\text{Avg total equity}} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Debt-to-assets shows the share of assets funded by debt; financial leverage (equity multiplier) is the DuPont leverage term.
formulas.trap: Reading financial leverage of 2.0 as debt equal to assets; it means assets are twice equity, so liabilities fund half.

formulas.name: Interest coverage and fixed charge coverage
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} \text{Interest coverage} = \frac{EBIT}{\text{Interest expense}} \\ \text{Fixed charge coverage} = \frac{EBIT + \text{Lease pmts}}{\text{Interest} + \text{Lease pmts}} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: Measure how many times operating earnings cover financing costs; fixed charge coverage adds lease payments to both lines.
formulas.trap: Adding lease payments only to the denominator; they were deducted in reaching EBIT, so they are added back on top too.

formulas.name: Gross and operating profit margin
formulas.use: Gross margin reflects pricing and production cost; operating margin also absorbs SG&A, R&D and other operating expenses.
formulas.trap: Judging profitability on gross margin alone; a rising gross margin with a falling operating margin means overheads outgrew sales.

formulas.name: Net profit margin and ROA
formulas.vars: ROA = net profit margin x total asset turnover; adjusted ROA adds back after-tax interest to NI
formulas.use: Net margin is profit kept per dollar of sales; ROA is net income per dollar of assets, however they are financed.
formulas.trap: Comparing ROA across firms with different leverage; interest cuts NI, so analysts may add after-tax interest back first.

formulas.name: Three-step DuPont ROE
formulas.vars: Terms cancel to ROE = NI / average total equity: net margin x asset turnover x financial leverage
formulas.use: Splits ROE into net margin, asset turnover and financial leverage to show whether returns come from operations or debt.
formulas.trap: Treating a higher ROE as always good; if only the leverage term rose, the gain came from more debt and higher risk.

formulas.name: Five-step DuPont ROE
formulas.vars: NI/EBT = tax burden; EBT/EBIT = interest burden; EBIT/Rev = EBIT margin; then asset turnover and equity multiplier
formulas.use: Separates ROE into tax burden, interest burden, EBIT margin, asset turnover and leverage to pinpoint what changed.
formulas.trap: Swapping the burdens: tax burden is NI/EBT, interest burden EBT/EBIT; a higher burden ratio means lower tax or interest cost.

formulas.name: Degree of operating leverage
formulas.vars: At a given sales level DOL also equals contribution margin / EBIT; more fixed operating cost means a higher DOL
formulas.use: Measures how far operating income moves for a given sales change, so fixed costs are modeled correctly in forecasts.
formulas.trap: Forecasting every cost as a fixed share of revenue, which forces DOL to 1 and understates both upside and downside.

definitions.def: Under IFRS 15 and ASC 606: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, set the transaction price, allocate it by relative standalone selling price, and recognize revenue as each obligation is satisfied.
A principal controls the good or service before transfer and reports revenue gross; an agent arranging another party's sale reports only its commission. Gross reporting inflates revenue, not profit.
A convertible, option or warrant whose assumed conversion or exercise would raise EPS or shrink a loss per share. It is excluded, so diluted EPS can never exceed basic EPS.
A disposed or held-for-sale component, reported net of tax below income from continuing operations. Unusual or infrequent items stay in continuing operations, though analysts often adjust them out.

definitions.term: Interest and dividend cash flow classification
definitions.def: US GAAP: interest paid and interest and dividends received are CFO; dividends paid are CFF. IFRS allows interest paid in CFO or CFF, receipts in CFO or CFI, and dividends paid in CFO or CFF.
Unqualified: fairly presented. Qualified: fair except for a specific material issue. Adverse: materially misstated. Disclaimer: the auditor could not gather enough evidence to form an opinion.

definitions.term: LIFO under IFRS vs US GAAP
definitions.def: LIFO is allowed under US GAAP but prohibited under IFRS. With rising prices LIFO gives higher COGS, lower profit and taxes, lower inventory and higher CFO than FIFO; weighted average falls in between.

IFRS: lower of cost and net realizable value, with reversals allowed up to original cost. US GAAP: lower of cost and NRV (lower of cost or market for LIFO and retail), and write-downs are never reversed.
Selling old, low-cost LIFO layers when quantities fall cuts COGS and lifts gross margin for one period only. A falling LIFO reserve flags it; strip the effect out of forecast margins.
Interest on constructing a long-lived asset is added to its cost and later depreciated. It shows as an investing outflow, lifting CFO; add it back to interest expense when computing coverage.

definitions.term: Impairment under IFRS vs US GAAP
definitions.def: US GAAP: impaired only if carrying amount exceeds undiscounted cash flows, then written to fair value, no reversal. IFRS: written to recoverable amount, the higher of FV less costs to sell and value in use; reversible.
IFRS expenses research but capitalizes development once technical feasibility and other criteria are met. US GAAP expenses both, except software for sale after technological feasibility.

definitions.term: Lessee accounting IFRS 16 vs US GAAP
definitions.def: Both record a right-of-use asset and lease liability. IFRS 16 expenses depreciation plus interest, front-loaded, with principal in CFF. A US GAAP operating lease books one straight-line cost, all in CFO.

Temporary differences between carrying amount and tax base reverse and create DTAs or DTLs. Permanent differences, such as tax-exempt income or non-deductible fines, never reverse and only move the effective rate.

A US GAAP contra account that reduces a DTA when realization is not more likely than not; IFRS recognizes a DTA only to the extent future taxable profit is probable. Releasing it lifts NI with no cash.

Revenue divided by average working capital: sales generated per dollar of working capital. It becomes meaningless when working capital is near zero or negative, so check the sign before comparing firms.

drill.why: Adding collection days and inventory days, then subtracting payment days, gives the cash conversion cycle. Each distractor converts a single turnover into days; none combines all three with DPO subtracted.

distractors: LIFO to FIFO: inventory and equity
Income tax expense and effective tax rate
drill.why: Subtracting the change in the LIFO reserve from COGS and adding its after-tax amount to NI restates the income statement to FIFO. The balance-sheet pair adds the ending reserve, not the change.
Adding after-tax interest back to CFO, then subtracting capex, gives cash available to all capital providers: FCFF. FCFE never adds interest back and instead adds net borrowing.

distractors: Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF)
drill.why: Subtracting capex from CFO and adding net borrowing leaves the cash available to common shareholders: FCFE. FCFF adds back after-tax interest and ignores net borrowing because it serves all capital providers.

distractors: Interest coverage and fixed charge coverage
drill.why: Five factors, with tax burden NI/EBT and interest burden EBT/EBIT ahead of EBIT margin, turnover and leverage, are the five-step DuPont. The three-step version uses net margin directly with no burden terms.

Cash plus marketable securities over current liabilities is the cash ratio; quick assets over daily cash expenditures give days of coverage, the defensive interval. The quick ratio divides the same assets by current liabilities.

distractors: Average age and remaining life of PP&E
drill.why: Twice the straight-line rate applied to opening book value, with no salvage subtracted, is double-declining balance. Straight-line and units of production divide cost minus salvage by life or by total units.

distractors: Income tax expense and effective tax rate
Funded status of a pension plan
drill.why: An asset's carrying amount above its tax base, times the tax rate, is tax owed later: the deferred tax liability. Income tax expense uses the year's changes in DTL and DTA, not the gap itself.

EBIT over interest expense is interest coverage; adding lease payments to both EBIT and interest gives fixed charge coverage. The cash flow version starts from CFO plus interest and taxes paid, not EBIT.

distractors: Interest coverage and fixed charge coverage
Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF)
drill.why: Adding interest and taxes paid back to CFO and dividing by interest paid gives cash flow interest coverage. EBIT-based interest coverage uses accrual earnings over interest expense instead of cash figures.

drill.drillLatex: \begin{gathered} ? = \frac{\text{Total debt}}{\text{Total assets}} \\ ? = \frac{\text{Avg total assets}}{\text{Avg total equity}} \end{gathered}
drill.why: Debt over total assets is debt-to-assets; average assets over average equity is the equity multiplier, or financial leverage. Debt-to-equity and debt-to-capital put debt over equity or over debt plus equity.

formulas.name: Return on a margin purchase
formulas.vars: Q = shares bought; Div = total dividends received; initial equity = initial margin x P_0 x Q; also subtract commissions if given
formulas.use: Return on the investor's own equity when part of the position is borrowed; leverage magnifies gains and losses.
formulas.trap: Dividing the gain by the full position value instead of the equity invested, or forgetting to subtract margin loan interest.

formulas.name: Leverage ratio of a margin position
formulas.use: Shows how many times price moves are magnified on the investor's equity at purchase, before interest (2.5x at 40% margin).
formulas.trap: Using 1/initial margin after the price has moved; once prices change, recompute position value over current equity.

formulas.name: Margin call price
formulas.use: Price at which equity falls to the maintenance margin and the investor must add funds (P_0 = 50, 40%/25% gives $40).
formulas.trap: Swapping the two margins, or assuming the call comes when the price has fallen by the initial margin percentage.

formulas.name: Price-weighted index value
formulas.vars: Divisor starts at N and is reset after splits and constituent changes so the index level does not jump
formulas.use: Index level for price-weighted indexes such as the DJIA and Nikkei 225; higher-priced stocks carry more weight.
formulas.trap: Leaving the divisor unchanged after a stock split; the divisor must be recomputed and the split stock's weight falls.

formulas.name: Market-capitalization weight
formulas.vars: Q_i = shares outstanding, or float (shares available to the public) for a float-adjusted index
formulas.use: Constituent weight in a cap-weighted index such as the S&P 500; weights move with prices, so no rebalancing is needed.
formulas.trap: Ignoring float adjustment for firms with large insider or government stakes, which overstates their index weight.

formulas.name: Equal weight
formulas.use: Constituent weight in an equal-weighted index; it tilts toward small caps and needs regular rebalancing as prices drift.
formulas.trap: Assuming weights stay at 1/N between rebalancing dates; winners drift above 1/N until the index rebalances.

formulas.name: Index return from constituent returns
formulas.vars: w_i = beginning-of-period weight: P_i / sum of prices (price-weighted), cap weight (value-weighted) or 1/N (equal-weighted)
formulas.use: Computes a one-period index return from constituent returns under any weighting method.
formulas.trap: Using end-of-period weights, or averaging returns equally for a price- or cap-weighted index.

formulas.name: Price return of an index
formulas.use: Return from changes in the index level only, as reported by price return indexes; excludes dividends and interest.
formulas.trap: Benchmarking a fund's total return against a price return index, which flatters the fund by roughly the dividend yield.

formulas.name: Total return of an index
formulas.vars: Inc_I = dividends or interest paid by constituents during the period
formulas.use: Return including the price change plus income paid by constituents; the fair benchmark for a fund's total return.
formulas.trap: Dividing income by the ending level V_1; total return = price return + income return, both measured over the starting level V_0.

formulas.name: Book value of equity
formulas.use: Accounting value of shareholders' residual claim; divide by shares outstanding for book value per share in P/B.
formulas.trap: Treating book value as market value; book equity reflects historical cost and omits unrecorded intangibles.

formulas.name: Return on equity (ROE)
formulas.vars: NI_t = net income to common shareholders; BV = book value of common equity (beginning BV is also used if average is not given)
formulas.use: Accounting return on shareholders' book equity; compare with the cost of equity to judge whether retention creates value.
formulas.trap: Treating ROE as the investor's required or expected return; ROE is accounting-based, the cost of equity is market-based.

formulas.name: Gordon growth model (constant-growth DDM)
formulas.vars: D_1 = next year's dividend = D_0(1 + g); r = required return on equity; valid only when r > g
formulas.use: Values a mature dividend payer growing at a constant rate forever; also the terminal value in multistage models.
formulas.trap: Putting D_0 in the numerator instead of D_1 = D_0(1 + g), or forcing a value when g is at or above r.

formulas.name: Required return implied by the Gordon model
formulas.use: Backs out the market-implied cost of equity from price, next dividend and growth: forward dividend yield plus growth.
formulas.trap: Using the trailing dividend D_0 in the yield term, which understates r by the growth in next year's dividend.

formulas.name: Two-stage dividend discount model
formulas.vars: D_1 to D_n grow at the high first-stage rate; g = constant long-run growth from year n + 1 onward
formulas.use: Values a firm with high near-term growth that settles into constant growth after year n.
formulas.trap: Discounting the terminal value n + 1 periods; D_{n+1}/(r - g) is a value at time n, so discount it n periods.

formulas.name: FCFE valuation model
formulas.vars: FCFE = CFO - FCInv + net borrowing; r = required return on equity; with constant growth, V_0 = FCFE_1 / (r - g)
formulas.use: Values equity from cash available to shareholders; suits firms that pay no or erratic dividends, or where a control buyer sets payout.
formulas.trap: Discounting FCFE at WACC; FCFE is a flow to equity only, so discount at the cost of equity. WACC pairs with FCFF.

formulas.name: Value of perpetual preferred stock
formulas.vars: D_p = fixed annual preferred dividend; r_p = required return on the preferred; rearranged, r_p = D_p / P_0
formulas.use: Values a fixed perpetual preferred dividend as a perpetuity; callable issues are worth less, putable ones more.
formulas.trap: Applying a growth rate to a fixed preferred dividend, or using the stated dividend rate instead of the market required return.

formulas.name: Sustainable growth rate
formulas.vars: b = retention ratio = 1 - dividend payout ratio
formulas.use: Growth the firm can fund from retained earnings without new equity or a change in leverage; a g input for the DDM.
formulas.trap: Using the payout ratio instead of the retention ratio b = 1 - payout.

formulas.name: Justified forward P/E
formulas.vars: D_1/E_1 = expected payout ratio = 1 - b
formulas.use: P/E implied by the Gordon model; it rises with payout and growth and falls as the required return rises.
formulas.trap: Putting the retention ratio b in the numerator instead of the payout ratio D_1/E_1 = 1 - b.

formulas.name: Justified trailing P/E
formulas.use: P/E on last year's earnings implied by the Gordon model; equals the justified forward P/E times (1 + g).
formulas.trap: Dropping the (1 + g) factor, which makes the trailing multiple equal to the forward one.

formulas.name: Justified price-to-book (P/B)
formulas.use: P/B implied by ROE, growth and required return; P/B above 1 is justified only when ROE exceeds the cost of equity.
formulas.trap: Writing ROE - r in the numerator; it is ROE - g over r - g.
formulas.vars: ROE = E_1 / B_0 on beginning book value; g = b x ROE; derived from the Gordon model with D_1 = (1 - b) x ROE x B_0

formulas.name: Implied price from a comparable multiple
formulas.vars: Metric must match the multiple: EPS for P/E, book value per share for P/B, sales per share for P/S
formulas.use: Method of comparables: applies a peer median multiple to the company's own per-share metric to judge relative value.
formulas.trap: Calling a stock cheap on a lower multiple without checking that growth, risk and accounting match the peers.

formulas.name: Price-to-sales and price-to-cash-flow
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} P/S = \frac{\text{Price}}{\text{Sales per share}} \\ P/CF = \frac{\text{Price}}{\text{Cash flow per share}} \end{gathered}
formulas.use: P/S suits firms with negative or volatile earnings; P/CF uses cash flow, which is harder to manipulate than earnings.
formulas.trap: Treating a low P/S as cheap regardless of margins; firms with equal sales can have very different profitability and cash flow.
formulas.vars: Cash flow = NI + D&A, CFO, FCFE or EBITDA per share, stated consistently across peers; market cap / revenue gives the same P/S

formulas.name: Enterprise value (EV)
formulas.vars: Pref = preferred stock; NCI = non-controlling interests; Cash = cash and short-term investments
formulas.use: Value of the operating business to all capital providers; the numerator for EV/EBITDA and EV/sales.
formulas.trap: Adding cash instead of subtracting it; borrowing and holding the cash leaves EV unchanged.

formulas.name: EV/EBITDA
formulas.use: Compares firms with different leverage and depreciation policies, since EBITDA is earned for all capital providers.
formulas.trap: Pairing market cap (an equity value) with EBITDA (a flow to all capital); the numerator must be EV.

formulas.name: PEG ratio
formulas.vars: g = expected EPS growth in percentage points (15, not 0.15)
formulas.use: P/E per point of expected growth; a lower PEG suggests a cheaper price for growth among firms of similar risk.
formulas.trap: Entering growth as a decimal (0.15 instead of 15), which inflates PEG one hundred times.

formulas.name: Asset-based equity value
formulas.use: Values firms whose worth sits in tangible or marketable assets: resource firms, financials, companies in liquidation.
formulas.trap: Using book values as if they were market values, or applying the method to intangible-heavy firms such as software.

definitions.def: Borrowing shares, selling them and buying them back later to return; the short seller pays the lender's dividends, posts margin and faces theoretically unlimited loss.
A market order executes immediately at the best available price but risks price impact; a limit order caps the price paid or received but may never execute.
A sell order that becomes a market order once the stock trades at or below the stop price, so in a gap or fast market it can fill well below the stop.
A broker is an agent who finds a counterparty for a commission; a dealer is a principal who trades from its own inventory and earns the bid-ask spread.
In the primary market the issuer sells new securities and receives the proceeds; in the secondary market investors trade existing securities and the issuer receives nothing.
Weights constituents by sales, earnings, book value or dividends rather than price, giving a contrarian value tilt versus market-cap weighting; needs periodic rebalancing.
Rebalancing resets the weights of existing constituents to target; reconstitution adds and deletes constituents. Both force index funds to trade.
Weak form: prices reflect past market data; semi-strong: all public information; strong: public and private information. Developed markets look semi-strong but not strong-form efficient.
A persistent return pattern inconsistent with efficiency, such as the January effect or momentum; many vanish after costs, risk adjustment or publication, or reflect data mining.
Preferred shares whose missed dividends accrue as arrears that must be paid before any common dividend; skipped non-cumulative preferred dividends are simply lost.
Sponsored receipts involve the foreign issuer and pass voting rights to holders; unsponsored receipts are created by a bank alone, which keeps the votes. Neither removes currency risk.
Threat of entrants, supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitutes and rivalry together set an industry's long-run profitability, not rivalry among competitors alone.
Embryonic, growth, shakeout, mature and decline stages: growth brings falling prices and rising profits, shakeout intense competition, maturity consolidation and high cash flow.
Cyclical industries (autos, construction) have earnings highly sensitive to the business cycle; defensive ones (utilities, staples) sell necessities with stable demand. Defensive is not low growth.
Top-down starts from macro or industry growth and applies the firm's market share; bottom-up builds from company drivers such as volume, price and new stores. Hybrids cross-check both.
Value estimated from fundamentals with a present value, multiplier or asset-based model; a stock is mispriced only if the gap to market price exceeds estimation error.

distractors: Required return implied by the Gordon model
drill.why: Next year's dividend capitalized at r minus g is the constant-growth DDM value. Preferred stock has no g in the denominator, and the justified forward P/E puts a payout ratio, not a dollar dividend, over r - g.
The expected payout ratio D1/E1 over r - g is the justified forward P/E. The trailing version uses D0/E0 times (1 + g); justified P/B puts ROE - g over the same denominator.
Last year's payout ratio grown one period, over r - g, is the P/E on trailing earnings E0. The forward P/E has no (1 + g) factor because D1/E1 already refers to next year.
ROE minus g over r minus g is the justified P/B, above 1 only when ROE beats r. The justified forward P/E shares the r - g denominator but has the payout ratio on top.

distractors: Leverage ratio of a margin position
drill.why: The loan per share P0(1 - initial margin) divided by 1 - maintenance margin is the price where equity hits the maintenance level. The leverage ratio uses only the initial margin and is a multiple, not a price.

distractors: Leverage ratio of a margin position
drill.why: Price gain plus dividends minus loan interest, over the investor's own equity, is the margin purchase return. An index total return adds income but has no interest cost and divides by the full starting value.

distractors: Required return implied by the Gordon model
drill.why: Change in level plus income, over the starting level, is the index total return. Price return drops the income term; the Gordon implied return is a forward dividend yield plus growth, not a realized return.
Retention ratio times ROE is the growth fundable from retained earnings without new equity. The classic slip is using the payout ratio; ROE alone is the return on book equity, not a growth rate.

Equity value plus debt, preferred and NCI, less cash, is the value of the operating business to all claimants: enterprise value. Book and asset-based equity values subtract liabilities instead of adding claims.

formulas.name: Callable and putable bond values
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} V_{\text{callable}} = V_{\text{straight}} - V_{\text{call}} \\ V_{\text{putable}} = V_{\text{straight}} + V_{\text{put}} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: V_straight = value of the otherwise identical option-free bond; the issuer owns the call, the investor owns the put
formulas.use: The investor is short the call (lower price, higher yield) and long the put (higher price, lower yield) versus a straight bond.
formulas.trap: Adding the call or subtracting the put; a callable never trades above, and a putable never below, its straight-bond value.

formulas.name: Repo loan amount after haircut
formulas.vars: Haircut (repo margin) = % of collateral market value the lender will not lend against; MV = market value of the collateral, not par
formulas.use: Sizes the cash raised by repo-ing securities; lower-quality, longer-dated or less liquid collateral carries a larger haircut.
formulas.trap: Lending against par or full market value; the haircut is deducted from market value, so the loan is always below the collateral value.

formulas.name: Repo interest
formulas.vars: r_repo = annual repo rate in decimal, usually quoted actual/360; repurchase price = loan + repo interest
formulas.use: Computes the borrower's financing cost and the repurchase price at the end of the repo term.
formulas.trap: Charging interest on the collateral value instead of the loan, or using 365 days when the repo rate is quoted actual/360.

formulas.name: Bond price with market discount rate (YTM)
formulas.vars: PMT = coupon per period; r = market discount rate per period (the YTM when solved for, given price); N = periods to maturity; priced on a coupon date
formulas.use: Prices an option-free bond on a coupon date, or solves for YTM as the IRR of the cash flows when the price is known.
formulas.trap: Mixing annual inputs with semiannual periods; PMT, r and N must all be per period, and the coupon rate is not the discount rate.

formulas.name: Full price and flat price between coupon dates
formulas.vars: PV = value at the last coupon date at the current yield; r = periodic yield; t = days since last coupon; T = days in the coupon period
formulas.use: Prices a bond between coupons: compound the last-coupon-date value forward, then strip accrued interest to get the quoted flat price.
formulas.trap: Settling at the quoted flat price; the buyer pays the full (dirty) price = flat + AI, and money duration and PVBP use the full price.

formulas.name: Accrued interest
