formulas.vars: t = days from last coupon to settlement; T = days in coupon period (actual/actual for governments, 30/360 for many corporates); PMT = periodic coupon
formulas.use: Computes the interest the buyer owes the seller for the part of the coupon period that has passed since the last coupon.
formulas.trap: Using the annual coupon on a semiannual bond, or counting days to the next coupon instead of days since the last one.

formulas.name: Current yield
formulas.use: Measures annual coupon income per unit of price; for a discount bond coupon rate < current yield < YTM, reversed for a premium bond.
formulas.trap: Treating current yield as total return; it ignores the pull to par and reinvestment, so it overstates the return on a premium bond.

formulas.name: Simple yield
formulas.vars: N = years to maturity; (Par - P_flat)/N = straight-line annual gain (discount bond) or loss, a negative number (premium bond)
formulas.use: Quick yield used for Japanese government bonds: the coupon plus straight-line amortization of the discount or premium, no compounding.
formulas.trap: Leaving out the amortized gain or loss (that is current yield), or compounding it like a YTM; simple yield amortizes in a straight line.

formulas.name: Yield periodicity conversion
formulas.vars: APR_m = annual yield quoted with m periods per year; APR_n = equivalent yield with n periods per year (n = 1 gives the effective annual yield)
formulas.use: Converts a yield to another compounding frequency, e.g. semiannual bond basis to annual, before comparing two bonds.
formulas.trap: Converting by simple scaling; 6% semiannual equals 6.09% annual, not 6%, because the compounding frequency changes the effective rate.

formulas.name: Money market discount rate
formulas.vars: Days = days to maturity; rearranged, PV = FV x (1 - Days/360 x DR)
formulas.use: Converts a T-bill or commercial paper price into its quoted discount rate, or a quoted discount rate into a price.
formulas.trap: Treating DR as a return; it divides by face value, not by price paid, and uses 360 days, so it understates the investor's yield.

formulas.name: Add-on rate and bond equivalent yield
formulas.vars: Year = 360 or 365 per the quote convention; with Year = 365 the add-on rate is the bond equivalent yield (BEY); PV = FV / (1 + Days/Year x AOR)
formulas.use: Computes a money market return on the amount invested (CDs, repos, SOFR); put every rate on a 365-day add-on basis before comparing.
formulas.trap: Comparing a discount rate with an add-on rate directly; convert first, and move an add-on rate from a 360 to a 365 basis by x 365/360.

formulas.name: Floating-rate note price with discount margin
formulas.vars: c = (MRR + QM)/m; d = (MRR + DM)/m; MRR = market reference rate (e.g. SOFR); QM = quoted margin; DM = discount margin; m = resets per year
formulas.use: Prices an FRN on a reset date from the quoted and required margins, or solves for the discount margin when the price is known.
formulas.trap: Discounting at MRR + QM; the coupon uses the quoted margin, the discount rate the required margin, so DM above QM puts the FRN below par.

formulas.name: Bond price with spot rates
formulas.vars: S_t = spot (zero-coupon) rate per period for maturity t; each cash flow is discounted at the rate for its own date
formulas.use: Gives the no-arbitrage price of a bond by valuing each cash flow as a separate zero-coupon bond.
formulas.trap: Discounting every cash flow at the longest spot rate or at the YTM; each cash flow gets the spot rate for its own maturity.

formulas.name: Bootstrapping spot rates from par rates
formulas.vars: PMT = N-period par rate x 100; S_1 to S_N-1 already solved from shorter par bonds; solve for S_N
formulas.use: Derives the next spot rate from a par bond priced at 100, using the spot rates already found for its earlier coupons.
formulas.trap: Using the par rate as the spot rate, or discounting the earlier coupons at S_N instead of at their own spot rates.

formulas.name: Implied forward rate
formulas.vars: f_A,B-A = rate starting in year A for B - A years (e.g. 2y3y); S_A, S_B = spot rates for A and B years, A < B
formulas.use: Finds the break-even future rate implied by two spot rates, e.g. the 1y1y rate from the 1-year and 2-year spot rates.
formulas.trap: Subtracting or averaging spot rates; forward rates come from compounding, and they are break-even rates, not forecasts.

formulas.name: Par rate from discount factors
formulas.vars: S_t = spot rate per period; result is the coupon rate per period at which an N-period bond prices at exactly par
formulas.use: Converts a spot curve into the par curve, the coupon an issuer would set today to price a new bond at 100.
formulas.trap: Reading a par rate as a spot rate; on an upward-sloping curve par rates sit slightly below spot rates because coupons come earlier.

formulas.name: G-spread
formulas.vars: YTM_gov = yield on a government bond of the same maturity, interpolated if no exact match exists
formulas.use: Measures a bond's yield premium over the government curve for credit, liquidity and tax differences at one benchmark point.
formulas.trap: Using an unmatched-maturity Treasury; interpolate the government yield to the bond's maturity before subtracting.

formulas.name: I-spread
formulas.vars: Swap rate = fixed rate on an interest rate swap of the same maturity and currency
formulas.use: Measures yield over the swap curve; used for bank bonds and by investors who fund or hedge at swap rates.
formulas.trap: Comparing one bond's I-spread with another bond's G-spread; the benchmarks differ, so the spreads are not on the same basis.

formulas.name: Z-spread (zero-volatility spread)
formulas.vars: S_t = government spot rate per period; Z = constant periodic spread added to every spot rate
formulas.use: Finds the constant spread over the whole government spot curve that reprices the bond; more accurate than G-spread on a steep curve.
formulas.trap: Thinking the Z-spread strips out embedded options; for a callable bond it still includes the option cost, which OAS removes.

formulas.name: Option-adjusted spread (OAS)
formulas.vars: Option cost in bp: positive for a callable bond (investor short a call), negative for a putable bond (investor long a put)
formulas.use: Removes the embedded option's value from the spread so callable, putable and straight bonds compare on credit and liquidity.
formulas.trap: Using a callable bond's Z-spread as its credit spread, which overstates compensation; for a putable bond OAS exceeds the Z-spread.

formulas.name: Macaulay duration
formulas.vars: t = time to each cash flow in periods; PV(CF_t) discounted at the YTM; weights sum to 1; result in periods (divide by periods per year for years)
formulas.use: Computes the PV-weighted average time to the bond's cash flows; the horizon that offsets price and reinvestment risk.
formulas.trap: Using Macaulay duration directly as price sensitivity; convert to modified duration first. Only a zero has D_Mac = maturity.

formulas.name: Modified duration
formulas.vars: r = yield per period (annual YTM / m). D_Mac in periods gives periodic D_Mod: divide by m to annualize. D_Mac in years gives annual D_Mod
formulas.use: Converts Macaulay duration into price sensitivity: the approximate % change in full price for a 1% (100 bp) change in yield.
formulas.trap: Dividing by (1 + annual yield) on a semiannual bond; use the periodic yield, then annualize a periodic duration by dividing by m.

formulas.name: Approximate modified duration
formulas.vars: PV_- / PV_+ = full price after the bond's own yield falls / rises by Delta Yield (annual, decimal, e.g. 0.001); PV_0 = current full price
formulas.use: Estimates annual modified duration by repricing the bond at a small yield bump each way; no closed-form formula needed.
formulas.trap: Dividing by Delta Yield instead of 2 x Delta Yield, or entering 10 bp as 10 rather than 0.001.

formulas.name: Approximate convexity
formulas.vars: Same three full prices and annual yield bump (decimal) as approximate modified duration
formulas.use: Estimates annual convexity, the curvature duration misses, from the same three prices used for approximate modified duration.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to square Delta Yield or dropping the 2PV_0 term; for an option-free bond the numerator is always positive.

formulas.name: Price change with duration and convexity
formulas.vars: D_Mod = annual modified duration; C = annual convexity; Delta y = yield change in decimal. Drop the second term for the duration-only estimate
formulas.use: Estimates the % change in full price for a yield change; the convexity term corrects duration for larger moves.
formulas.trap: Subtracting the convexity term when yields rise or dropping the 1/2; (Delta y)^2 is positive, so positive convexity always adds.

formulas.name: Money duration
formulas.vars: D_Mod = annual modified duration; PV_Full = position market value at full price (incl. accrued interest), not par; Delta PV = -MoneyDur x Delta y
formulas.use: Converts percentage sensitivity into currency for a position, the figure hedgers and risk managers use to size trades.
formulas.trap: Reading money duration as a % or as the loss per 1%; it is currency per unit change in yield, so multiply by 0.01 for a 100 bp move.

formulas.name: Price value of a basis point (PVBP)
formulas.vars: Same as DV01: currency change per 1 bp; equals MoneyDur x 0.0001, or (PV_- - PV_+)/2 for a 1 bp bump in yield
formulas.use: Gives the currency change in a position's value for a 1 bp yield change; used to size hedges and compare positions.
formulas.trap: Using par or flat price instead of full market value, or the 1% scale (x 0.01) instead of the 1 bp scale (x 0.0001).

formulas.name: Effective duration
formulas.vars: Delta Curve = parallel shift of the benchmark yield curve (decimal); PV_- / PV_+ come from a model that lets cash flows change (calls, prepayments)
formulas.use: Measures sensitivity to a parallel benchmark-curve shift for bonds with embedded options and MBS, where yield duration fails.
formulas.trap: Using yield-based modified duration for a callable bond or MBS; their cash flows change with rates, so only effective duration works.

formulas.name: Effective convexity
formulas.vars: Same model prices and benchmark-curve shift as effective duration
formulas.use: Measures curvature for bonds with embedded options; a callable bond priced near its call price shows negative effective convexity.
formulas.trap: Assuming convexity is always positive; when PV_- + PV_+ < 2PV_0 (callables at low yields, MBS) effective convexity is negative.

formulas.name: Portfolio duration
formulas.vars: w_i = bond i's share of portfolio market value (full price); D_i = each bond's modified or effective duration
formulas.use: Approximates portfolio duration as the market-value-weighted average of bond durations; valid for parallel curve shifts.
formulas.trap: Weighting by par value, or assuming the weighted average captures risk from non-parallel moves such as steepening.

formulas.name: Key rate durations
formulas.vars: KeyRateDur_k = % price change for a 100 bp shift at curve maturity k only, all other key rates held constant
formulas.use: Splits effective duration across curve points to show exposure to steepening, flattening and twists.
formulas.trap: Assuming equal effective durations mean equal risk; a barbell and a bullet with the same duration react differently to a twist.

formulas.name: Duration gap
formulas.vars: D_Mac and investment horizon both in years
formulas.use: Shows which risk dominates: a positive gap means price risk dominates (rising rates hurt); negative means reinvestment risk dominates.
formulas.trap: Using modified duration in the gap; the horizon match that offsets price and reinvestment risk uses Macaulay duration.

formulas.name: Expected loss
formulas.vars: PD (or POD) = probability of default over the period; RR = recovery rate; LGD = loss given default, % of exposure
formulas.use: Computes the expected credit loss per period as a % of exposure, the minimum the credit spread must cover.
formulas.trap: Multiplying PD by the recovery rate instead of LGD; with 40% recovery, LGD is 60%.

formulas.name: Credit spread approximation
formulas.vars: PD and LGD per year in decimal; the spread is over a default-free benchmark of the same maturity
formulas.use: Links spread to default risk: a 2% annual PD with 60% LGD implies a spread of roughly 120 bp.
formulas.trap: Using the recovery rate instead of LGD, or a multi-year cumulative PD; spread is about annual PD x (1 - recovery rate).

formulas.name: Leverage and coverage ratios
formulas.vars: FFO = funds from operations: net income from continuing operations + D&A + deferred taxes + other non-cash items
formulas.use: Assesses capacity, the first C of credit analysis; these leverage and coverage ratios drive issuer ratings and covenant tests.
formulas.trap: Reading every ratio the same way; a higher Debt/EBITDA means weaker credit, while higher FFO/Debt or EBITDA/Interest means stronger.

formulas.name: Single monthly mortality (SMM)
formulas.vars: CPR = conditional prepayment rate (annualized); SMM = share of the month's balance, after scheduled principal, that is prepaid
formulas.use: Converts an annual prepayment speed into the monthly rate used to project MBS principal cash flows.
formulas.trap: Dividing CPR by 12; prepayments compound on a shrinking balance, so the monthly rate is 1 - (1 - CPR)^(1/12).

definitions.def: Affirmative covenants require the issuer to act (pay taxes, maintain insurance, report); negative covenants forbid actions such as extra debt, asset sales or excess dividends that weaken bondholders' claims.
A provision requiring the issuer to retire part of the issue on a schedule. It lowers credit risk, but bonds are often called at par, so investors face reinvestment risk when rates have fallen.

On a floating-rate note the quoted margin is the fixed spread over the reference rate in the coupon; the discount margin is the spread investors now require. A discount margin above the quoted margin puts it below par.

Estimating the price of an illiquid or new bond from yields on comparable bonds of similar credit, coupon and maturity, interpolating linearly between maturities and discounting at the interpolated yield.

definitions.term: Yield to call and yield to worst
definitions.def: Yield to call is the IRR assuming redemption at a call date and call price. Yield to worst is the lowest of the YTM and every yield to call, a conservative measure that still ignores option value.
With the yield unchanged, a premium bond's price falls and a discount bond's price rises toward par as maturity nears (constant-yield price trajectory), reaching par at maturity.
Pure expectations theory treats forward rates as unbiased forecasts of future short rates; liquidity preference adds a term premium, so an upward-sloping curve need not signal rising rates.
Price behavior of callable bonds and MBS at low yields: gains are capped as rates fall (call or prepayment) while losses continue as rates rise, so effective convexity is below zero.

Duration estimated by regressing a bond's price changes on benchmark yield changes. For high-yield bonds it is often below analytical duration because spreads tend to widen when government yields fall.
Ratings of BBB- (S&P, Fitch) or Baa3 (Moody's) and above are investment grade; BB+/Ba1 and below are high yield. A bond downgraded across that line is a fallen angel and may face forced selling.
Adjusting an issue rating up or down from the issuer's senior unsecured rating to reflect seniority and expected recovery, so an issuer's subordinated debt is rated below its secured debt.
Contraction risk: rates fall, prepayments speed up and principal returns early to be reinvested at lower rates. Extension risk: rates rise, prepayments slow and the security's life lengthens.

Internal enhancement is built into the deal: subordination (losses hit junior tranches first), overcollateralization, excess spread, reserve accounts. External relies on a third party: a guarantee or letter of credit.

A covered bond stays on the bank's balance sheet with dual recourse to the issuer and a dynamic cover pool whose bad assets must be replaced; an ABS investor relies only on assets sold to a bankruptcy-remote SPE.

drill.why: Dividing the gain by PV, the amount invested, and annualizing on a 360- or 365-day year gives the add-on rate (the BEY on 365). The discount rate divides the same gain by face value and uses 360.

distractors: Add-on rate and bond equivalent yield
drill.why: Dividing the dollar discount by face value and annualizing on 360 days is the money market discount rate. The add-on rate divides by PV, the amount invested, so it is higher for the same bill.

distractors: Bond price with market discount rate (YTM)
drill.why: Adding straight-line amortization of the discount or premium to the coupon gives simple yield. Current yield stops at coupon over price; YTM compounds the pull to par instead of spreading it evenly.

distractors: Bootstrapping spot rates from par rates
drill.why: Two spot rates compounded to different horizons pin down the rate between them, the implied forward rate. Periodicity conversion equates one horizon under two compounding frequencies, not two horizons.
One constant added to every government spot rate until PV equals price is the Z-spread. Plain spot-rate pricing adds no spread, and the G-spread compares one yield with one benchmark yield.
Subtracting the embedded option's cost from the Z-spread leaves the option-adjusted spread. The Z-spread itself still contains the option cost; the I-spread is a yield minus a swap rate.

Dividing Macaulay duration by one plus the periodic yield turns time-weighted duration into price sensitivity, modified duration. Approximate modified duration reaches a similar number from bumped prices.

The bump is in the bond's own yield, so this is approximate modified duration. Effective duration has the same shape but shifts the benchmark curve and lets cash flows change; convexity adds PV_- and PV_+.
Adding the up and down prices and subtracting 2PV_0 measures curvature, and a benchmark-curve shift makes it effective convexity. Approximate convexity bumps the bond's own yield instead.

distractors: Price change with duration and convexity
drill.why: Money duration scaled by 0.0001 gives the currency change for one basis point, the PVBP. Without the 0.0001 it is money duration, stated per unit (100%) change in yield.

Subtracting the holding period from Macaulay duration gives the duration gap; positive means price risk dominates. Portfolio duration is a weighted average of durations, not a comparison with a horizon.

Probability of default times loss given default is expected loss as a % of exposure. The credit spread approximation uses the same product, but observed spreads also carry risk and liquidity premiums.

formulas.name: Forward price, no income or costs
formulas.vars: S_0 = spot price today; r = annual risk-free rate (periodic compounding); T = years to expiration
formulas.use: Prices a forward on an asset with no income or carrying costs by cost of carry: buy spot today and finance it to delivery.
formulas.trap: Setting F_0(T) equal to the expected future spot price; the forward is set by no-arbitrage at the risk-free rate, not by forecasts.

formulas.name: Forward price with income and costs
formulas.vars: PV_I = present value of income or benefits (dividends, coupons, convenience yield); PV_C = present value of storage and other carrying costs
formulas.use: Prices a forward when the underlying pays income or has carrying costs, such as dividend stocks, bonds or stored commodities.
formulas.trap: Adding income instead of subtracting it; the spot holder, not the forward long, receives the income, so it lowers the forward price.

formulas.name: Forward price, continuous compounding
formulas.vars: r = continuously compounded risk-free rate; c = continuous cost-of-carry rate (storage); i = continuous income or convenience yield rate
formulas.use: Prices a forward when the risk-free rate, costs and yields are quoted as continuously compounded annual rates.
formulas.trap: Plugging an annually compounded rate into the exponent, or adding the income yield i instead of subtracting it.

formulas.name: Forward value during its life (long)
formulas.vars: S_t = spot price at time t; F_0(T) = forward price locked in at inception; T - t = years remaining to expiration
formulas.use: Marks a long forward to market before expiration; the value is zero at inception and the short's value is the negative.
formulas.trap: Using S_t - F_0(T) without discounting before expiry; with income or costs, also adjust S_t by the PV of those remaining flows.

formulas.name: Forward value at expiration (long)
formulas.use: Gives the long forward's settlement value at expiration; the short receives the mirror image, F_0(T) - S_T.
formulas.trap: Using today's forward price for a new contract instead of the price locked in at inception, or still discounting at expiration.

formulas.name: Futures basis
formulas.vars: S_t = spot price of the exposure; F_t = price of the hedging futures contract at the same date
formulas.use: Measures spot minus futures for a hedge; the change in basis is the part of the price a futures hedger cannot lock in.
formulas.trap: Reversing the sign to futures minus spot; a long hedger benefits when the basis weakens and a short hedger when it strengthens.

formulas.name: FRA fixed rate (implied forward rate)
formulas.vars: R_A, R_B = annualized money market rates to the FRA start (t_A) and end (t_B), with t in years on the quoted day-count basis (usually days/360)
formulas.use: Sets the fixed rate of an FRA as the implied forward rate for the period between t_A and t_B.
formulas.trap: Quoting the longer spot rate R_B as the FRA rate, or annualizing by dividing by t_B instead of the FRA period t_B - t_A.

formulas.name: FRA settlement payment (long, pay fixed)
formulas.vars: MRR = market reference rate set at the FRA start; t = FRA period in years (days/360); NA = notional amount
formulas.use: Cash settlement to the pay-fixed (long) FRA party when it settles at the start of the period, so it is discounted at MRR.
formulas.trap: Forgetting the 1 + MRR t discount for settlement in advance, or giving the long a gain when MRR falls below the FRA rate.

formulas.name: Swap fixed rate (par swap rate)
formulas.vars: DF_i = discount factor for payment date i; N = number of fixed payments; the result is a per-period rate, so multiply by payments per year to annualize
formulas.use: Finds the fixed rate that equates PV of fixed and floating legs, giving the swap zero value at inception.
formulas.trap: Averaging spot rates; the swap rate is the par yield of a bond priced off the same discount factors.

formulas.name: Swap value after initiation (pay fixed)
formulas.vars: s_new, s_fixed = current and original fixed rates per period (annual rate / payments per year); DF_i = current discount factors for the remaining dates
formulas.use: Values a pay-fixed swap after inception as the PV of the fixed-rate difference over the remaining payments.
formulas.trap: Reversing the sign: the fixed payer gains when the current swap rate rises above the rate it locked in.

formulas.name: Option value: exercise value plus time value
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} c_0 = \max(0, S_0 - X) + \text{time value} \\ p_0 = \max(0, X - S_0) + \text{time value} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: c_0, p_0 = call and put premiums; S_0 = current price of the underlying; X = exercise (strike) price
formulas.use: Splits a premium into exercise (intrinsic) value and time value; time value decays to zero at expiration.
formulas.trap: Calling an out-of-the-money option worthless before expiry; its whole premium is time value.

formulas.name: Long call profit at expiration
formulas.use: Long call profit at expiration: breakeven S_T = X + c_0, maximum loss c_0; the writer's profit is the negative.
formulas.trap: Confusing payoff with profit by leaving out the premium, or forgetting that the call writer's potential loss is unlimited.

formulas.name: Long put profit at expiration
formulas.use: Long put profit at expiration: breakeven S_T = X - p_0, maximum loss p_0, maximum profit X - p_0 if S_T = 0.
formulas.trap: Treating the put buyer's upside as unlimited; it is capped at X - p_0 because the price cannot fall below zero.

formulas.name: Covered call profit
formulas.use: Long stock plus short call: maximum gain X - S_0 + c_0, breakeven S_0 - c_0; trades upside for premium income.
formulas.trap: Thinking the short call protects the downside; the maximum loss is still S_0 - c_0, cushioned only by the premium.

formulas.name: Protective put profit
formulas.use: Long stock plus long put: maximum loss S_0 - X + p_0, breakeven S_0 + p_0, upside unlimited; works like insurance.
formulas.trap: Leaving the put premium out of the maximum loss or the breakeven; the insurance cost p_0 is paid in every outcome.

formulas.name: Put-call parity
formulas.use: Fiduciary call equals protective put; prices a European put from the call (or vice versa) and builds synthetic positions.
formulas.trap: Using the undiscounted strike; X is paid at expiry, so it must be discounted, and parity holds only for European options.

formulas.name: Put-call-forward parity
formulas.use: Links European calls and puts to a forward on the same underlying; when F_0(T) = X, the call and put cost the same.
formulas.trap: Leaving F_0(T) undiscounted; the forward price is paid at T, so both F_0(T) and X are discounted at the risk-free rate.

formulas.name: Risk-neutral probability
formulas.vars: u, d = gross up and down factors (S_u = uS_0, S_d = dS_0); r = risk-free rate for the period
formulas.use: Gives the risk-neutral probability of an up move in a one-period binomial tree, used to value the option.
formulas.trap: Substituting the real-world probability of an up move; it plays no role in no-arbitrage option pricing.

formulas.name: One-period binomial option value
formulas.vars: c_u, c_d = option payoffs after an up and a down move; the same form values a European put with p_u and p_d
formulas.use: Values a European option as the risk-neutral expected payoff discounted one period at the risk-free rate.
formulas.trap: Discounting at a risky rate or the stock's expected return; risk-neutral expectations are always discounted at r.

formulas.name: Hedge ratio and replicating portfolio
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} h = \frac{c_u - c_d}{S_u - S_d} \\ c_0 = h\,S_0 + \frac{c_d - h\,S_d}{1+r} \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: h = shares per option; S_u, S_d = stock prices after up and down moves; for a call, c_d - hS_d < 0 means borrowing
formulas.use: Replicates a call with h shares plus borrowing; long h shares and short one call is risk-free and earns r.
formulas.trap: Inverting the ratio (stock spread over option spread); h is the option payoff range divided by the stock price range.

definitions.def: A forward commitment (forward, futures, swap) obliges both sides to transact, so the payoff is symmetric and no premium is paid. A contingent claim (option, CDS) gives a right, not an obligation, for a premium.
Exchange-traded contracts are standardized, centrally cleared and margined daily. OTC contracts are customized and bilateral, although many standard OTC swaps must now be centrally cleared.
A derivative is priced off a replicating portfolio of the underlying and risk-free borrowing or lending, so its price does not depend on risk preferences or the expected future spot price.

Futures are standardized, exchange-traded and settled daily through margin; forwards are customized OTC contracts settled at expiry. Prices match if interest rates are constant or uncorrelated with the underlying.
When a futures account falls below the maintenance margin, the trader must deposit variation margin to bring it back to the initial margin, not merely to the maintenance level.
The risk that the basis (spot minus futures) changes unexpectedly because the hedge contract, date or location differs from the exposure, so a futures hedge never locks in a price exactly.

definitions.term: Swap as a series of forwards
definitions.def: A plain vanilla swap is a portfolio of forward contracts (FRAs) all struck at one fixed rate. Each forward may have nonzero value, but the swap rate makes their combined value zero at inception.
Exchanges principal in two currencies at the start and at maturity, plus interest in each currency in between. Unlike an interest rate swap, notional is usually exchanged, adding currency risk.
A call is in the money when S > X and out of the money when S < X; a put is the reverse, and S = X is at the money. Moneyness sets exercise value, not the full premium.
Higher S, volatility, time and interest rates raise call values; higher X and dividends lower them. For puts the effects flip, except volatility and usually time, which raise both.
A European option can be exercised only at expiration; an American option at any time before. Put-call parity and the binomial formulas on this sheet apply to European options.

distractors: Forward price, no income or costs
drill.why: Spot net of income PV plus cost PV, compounded at r, is the forward price with carry. The no-income version has no PV terms; the continuous version uses e^{(r+c-i)T}; forward value subtracts a discounted forward price.

distractors: Forward price, no income or costs
drill.why: Current spot minus the discounted locked-in forward price is the long's value before expiry. At expiration nothing is discounted (S_T - F_0(T)); basis subtracts the current futures price, not a present value.

distractors: Forward price, no income or costs
drill.why: Long-period growth over short-period growth, annualized over t_B - t_A, is the implied forward rate that sets the FRA. The settlement payment instead multiplies MRR - FRA by notional and discounts it.

One minus the final discount factor over the sum of discount factors is the par rate that gives a new swap zero value. Swap value after initiation multiplies a rate difference by notional and the DF sum.

Call plus discounted strike (fiduciary call) equals put plus stock (protective put), with spot S_0 itself on the right. Put-call-forward parity replaces S_0 with the discounted forward price F_0(T)/(1+r)^T.

distractors: Forward price, no income or costs
drill.why: A discounted forward price stands in for the stock in the protective put, so this is put-call-forward parity. Put-call parity uses S_0 directly; forward value subtracts the discounted forward price from spot.

Gross risk-free return minus the down factor over the up-down spread is the risk-neutral probability. The hedge ratio also has a spread denominator but divides option payoffs by stock prices, not factors.
Stock gain plus the call premium received, minus the payoff owed to the call buyer, is a covered call. A protective put pays a premium (-p_0) and adds a put payoff max(0, X - S_T).

distractors: Option value: exercise value plus time value
drill.why: Put payoff max(0, X - S_T) less the premium paid is the long put's profit. The long call reverses S_T and X; the protective put also includes the stock's gain S_T - S_0.

formulas.name: Incentive fee, hard vs soft hurdle
formulas.latex: \begin{gathered} IF_{hard} = p \times \max(0,\; G - h\,V_0) \\ IF_{soft} = p \times G \;\text{ if }\; G \ge h\,V_0 \end{gathered}
formulas.vars: p = incentive fee rate; G = gain for the period (net of the management fee if the terms say so); h = hurdle rate; V_0 = starting capital
formulas.use: Computes the performance fee when a hurdle applies: a hard hurdle pays only on the gain above it, a soft one on the whole gain.
formulas.trap: Charging a soft-hurdle fee only on the excess over the hurdle, or paying any incentive fee when the return misses the hurdle.

formulas.name: Incentive fee with high-water mark
formulas.vars: V_1 = ending NAV before fees; MF = management fee, deducted first when the incentive fee is net of it; HWM = highest prior NAV on which an incentive fee was paid
formulas.use: Limits the incentive fee to gains above the high-water mark so investors do not pay twice for the same gains.
formulas.trap: Charging the fee on a rebound that is still below the mark, or resetting the mark lower after a losing year.

formulas.name: Net return after fees
formulas.vars: V_1 = gross ending value; MF = management fee (rate x AUM on beginning or ending assets, per terms); IF = incentive fee; V_0 = starting value
formulas.use: Converts gross fund performance into the investor's return after management and incentive fees.
formulas.trap: Charging the incentive fee on the gross gain when terms say net of the management fee: 20% x 20 instead of 20% x 18.

formulas.name: Leveraged return on equity
formulas.vars: V_c = investor's own cash; V_b = borrowed funds; r = return on the total position; r_b = borrowing rate
formulas.use: Computes the return on the investor's own capital when part of the position is financed by borrowing.
formulas.trap: Dividing by total assets V_c + V_b instead of own capital V_c, which hides how leverage magnifies gains and losses.

formulas.name: Sortino ratio
formulas.vars: R_target = minimum acceptable return (often R_f or 0); sigma_down = downside deviation, using only returns below the target
formulas.use: Ranks alternative managers on excess return per unit of downside risk, suited to skewed hedge fund returns.
formulas.trap: Using total standard deviation as in the Sharpe ratio; Sortino penalizes only returns that fall below the target.

formulas.name: Calmar ratio
formulas.vars: Maximum drawdown = largest peak-to-trough cumulative loss, typically measured over the last 36 months
formulas.use: Compares return with the worst peak-to-trough loss, a common risk check for hedge funds and managed futures.
formulas.trap: Putting volatility in the denominator; Calmar divides by maximum drawdown, which captures sequential losses that sigma hides.

formulas.name: MOIC (multiple of invested capital)
formulas.use: Measures total value returned per dollar paid into a private fund, realized distributions plus unrealized holdings.
formulas.trap: Ranking funds on MOIC alone; it ignores timing, so 2.0x over 4 years is a far higher IRR than 2.0x over 10 years.

formulas.name: IRR, single entry and exit
formulas.vars: n = years held; exit equity = exit enterprise value minus remaining net debt
formulas.use: Annualizes a buyout return when there is one investment and one exit with no interim cash flows.
formulas.trap: Using enterprise values instead of equity values, which understates the return that leverage and debt paydown add.

formulas.name: Post-money valuation (venture capital)
formulas.vars: Ownership share = fraction of the company the new investor receives, in decimals
formulas.use: Values a start-up after a funding round from the new investment and the stake it buys.
formulas.trap: Dividing by existing holders' share instead of the new stake: $5 million for 20% implies $25 million post-money, not $6.25 million.

formulas.name: Pre-money valuation (venture capital)
formulas.use: Values the start-up before the new cash; a pre-money below the prior round's post-money signals a down round.
formulas.trap: Adding the investment to post-money instead of subtracting it; pre-money excludes the new cash, post-money includes it.

formulas.name: Net operating income (NOI)
formulas.vars: Vacancy = vacancy and collection losses; OpEx = property taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities; excludes debt service, depreciation and income taxes
formulas.use: Measures a property's unlevered operating income, the input to cap rate valuation and debt coverage.
formulas.trap: Subtracting mortgage interest or depreciation; NOI is measured before financing costs and income taxes.

formulas.name: Direct capitalization value
formulas.vars: NOI_1 = expected NOI for the next year; cap rate = NOI / value observed in comparable sales
formulas.use: Values a stabilized income property under the income approach by capitalizing next year's NOI.
formulas.trap: Thinking a higher cap rate means a higher value; value falls when cap rates rise, for example as interest rates increase.

formulas.name: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR)
formulas.vars: Debt service = annual mortgage payments, interest plus scheduled principal
formulas.use: Tests whether a property's NOI covers its mortgage payments; lenders set a minimum above 1.0x.
formulas.trap: Using interest only in the denominator; debt service includes the scheduled principal repayment.

formulas.name: Loan-to-value ratio (LTV)
formulas.use: Measures mortgage leverage on a property; a higher LTV means more leverage and a thinner equity cushion.
formulas.trap: Dividing the loan by the equity invested, which gives a debt-to-equity ratio, instead of by total property value.

formulas.name: Commodity futures total return
formulas.vars: R_spot = change in spot price; R_roll = gain or loss from rolling expiring contracts; R_collateral = interest on cash collateral
formulas.use: Breaks a fully collateralized commodity futures position's return into spot, roll and collateral components.
formulas.trap: Treating a commodity index return as the spot price change and leaving out roll and collateral returns.

formulas.name: Roll return
formulas.vars: F_near = price of the expiring contract sold; F_far = price of the longer-dated contract bought; CFA convention divides by F_near
formulas.use: Measures the gain or loss from rolling a long futures position: positive in backwardation, negative in contango.
formulas.trap: Getting the sign backward: in contango F_far > F_near, so roll return is negative; also dividing by F_far instead of F_near.

definitions.def: Illiquidity and lockups, specialized managers, leverage, limited regulation and transparency, high performance-based fees, and short or smoothed return histories. Main roles: diversification and return.
Fund investing has the highest fees and least control; co-investing alongside a fund cuts fees and adds control; direct investing gives full control and lowest fees but needs a large in-house team.
The general partner runs the fund with unlimited liability; limited partners commit capital drawn through capital calls. Management fees often run on committed capital during the investment period.
Appraisal-based values lag and smooth true price changes, understating volatility and correlation with public markets. Using reported figures in optimization over-allocates to illiquid assets.
A fund of funds charges its own management and incentive fees on top of the underlying funds' fees. Underlying 2/20 plus a 1/10 FoF layer can cut a 10% gross return to about 5% net.
The GP's share of fund profits, typically 20%, earned once LPs recover capital and any preferred return under a whole-of-fund waterfall. It is a profit share, unlike the management fee on capital.
A European (whole-of-fund) waterfall pays carry only after LPs receive all contributed capital plus preferred return; an American (deal-by-deal) waterfall pays carry on each exit, favoring the GP.
A contractual term requiring the GP to return carried interest already received if, at fund end, LPs have not received their capital plus preferred return. Without the clause there is no clawback.
Survivorship bias: failed funds stop reporting and drop out of indexes. Backfill bias: funds join after strong starts and add their past returns. Both inflate reported hedge fund index returns.
Early in a private fund's life, fees and write-downs make cumulative returns negative; they turn positive as investments mature and exit. Committing across vintage years smooths the effect.

definitions.term: Buyout vs venture vs growth equity
definitions.def: LBOs buy mature cash-generating firms with heavy debt; venture capital funds early-stage firms where a few winners drive returns; growth equity takes minority stakes in growing firms with little leverage.
A listed vehicle that avoids corporate tax by distributing most taxable income (90% in the US). REITs are liquid but track equities and rates short term, unlike appraisal-based private property.

Brownfield assets already operate with established cash flows; greenfield projects are new builds with construction and demand risk. Availability payments cut demand risk versus usage fees such as tolls.
Contango: longer-dated futures priced above near-dated, so rolling a long position loses. Backwardation: longer-dated below near-dated, so rolling gains. Neither is a forecast of the spot price.

Equity hedge (long/short), event-driven (merger arbitrage, distressed), relative value (convertible, fixed income arbitrage), opportunistic (global macro, managed futures), specialist (volatility) and multi-manager.

Assets recorded on distributed ledgers, permissionless (Bitcoin) or permissioned. Cryptocurrencies have no cash flows, stablecoins target a reference asset, and tokenization records ownership of real assets.

distractors: Incentive fee, hard vs soft hurdle
drill.why: The fee rate applies only to value above the highest NAV already charged, so this is the high-water mark fee. A hurdle fee compares the gain with h x V_0, a return threshold, not a prior peak NAV.

Return on the whole position minus interest on borrowed funds, divided by the investor's own cash, is the leveraged return. Net return after fees subtracts fees from a gross value and divides by starting value.
Excess return over a target divided by downside deviation is the Sortino ratio. Calmar also targets downside risk but divides annualized return by the maximum drawdown, not by a deviation measure.
Realized plus unrealized value per dollar paid in is MOIC, a multiple with no time dimension. The single-exit IRR takes the equity multiple to the power 1/n to annualize it.
Grossing up the new investment by the stake it buys gives the post-money value, which includes the new cash. Pre-money then subtracts that investment from post-money.
NOI over annual mortgage payments measures how many times income covers debt service. Direct capitalization also divides NOI but by the cap rate, producing a value, not a coverage multiple.

formulas.name: Expected portfolio return
formulas.vars: w_i = portfolio weight of asset i (weights sum to 1); E(R_i) = expected return of asset i
formulas.use: Gives a portfolio's expected return as the weighted average of its assets' expected returns.
formulas.trap: Applying the same weighted average to standard deviation; return averages linearly, risk does not unless correlation is 1.

formulas.name: Utility of an investment
formulas.vars: A = risk aversion coefficient (A > 0 risk-averse, A = 0 risk-neutral, A < 0 risk-seeking); E(R) and sigma in decimals
formulas.use: Ranks portfolios for an investor with risk aversion A; pick the highest utility, not the highest expected return.
formulas.trap: Plugging in percentages (10 and 20) instead of decimals, or forgetting to square the standard deviation.

formulas.name: Covariance from correlation
formulas.use: Converts a correlation into covariance for the portfolio variance and beta formulas, or backs out rho from covariance.
formulas.trap: Inserting covariance where a formula already shows rho x sigma_1 x sigma_2, which multiplies by the volatilities twice.

formulas.name: Two-asset portfolio variance
formulas.use: Computes two-asset portfolio risk; take the square root for sigma_p, which falls below the weighted-average sigma when rho < 1.
formulas.trap: Averaging the two sigmas and dropping the cross term, or forgetting the factor 2 on the covariance term.

formulas.name: Diversification benefit when correlation < 1
formulas.use: States when combining two assets lowers risk below the weighted-average sigma; at rho = 1 the two are equal.
formulas.trap: Thinking diversification can remove all risk in a large portfolio; it removes unsystematic risk but leaves market risk.

formulas.name: Equal-weighted portfolio variance (N assets)
formulas.vars: sigma-bar squared = average asset variance; Cov-bar = average pairwise covariance; N = number of equally weighted assets
formulas.use: Shows that as N grows the average-variance term fades and portfolio variance approaches the average covariance.
formulas.trap: Expecting portfolio risk to reach zero as N grows; it converges to the average covariance, the undiversifiable part.

formulas.name: Expected return of a risk-free and risky mix
formulas.vars: w_i = weight in risky portfolio i; w_i > 1 means borrowing at R_f, so 1 - w_i is negative
formulas.use: Gives the expected return of a point on the CAL from the weight in the risky portfolio, including leveraged positions.
formulas.trap: Capping w_i at 1; a borrowing investor has w_i > 1 and a negative risk-free weight, which raises both return and sigma.

formulas.name: Standard deviation on the CAL
formulas.vars: w_i = weight in risky portfolio i (above 1 means borrowing at R_f); the risk-free asset has sigma = 0 and zero covariance
formulas.use: Gives the risk of a mix of a risky portfolio and the risk-free asset; solve w_i = target sigma / sigma_i.
formulas.trap: Running the full two-asset variance formula; with a risk-free asset there is no cross term, so risk is linear in w_i.

formulas.name: Capital allocation line (CAL)
formulas.vars: i = the risky portfolio combined with the risk-free asset; sigma_p = standard deviation of the combined portfolio
formulas.use: Expected return of any mix of the risk-free asset and risky portfolio i; the slope is that portfolio's Sharpe ratio.
formulas.trap: Putting beta on the x-axis; the CAL and CML are plotted against total risk sigma, the SML against beta.

formulas.name: Capital market line (CML)
formulas.use: The CAL through the market (tangency) portfolio; gives expected return of efficient portfolios by total risk.
formulas.trap: Pricing an individual stock on the CML; single assets are inefficient and are priced by beta on the SML.

formulas.name: Total risk decomposition
formulas.vars: beta_i^2 sigma_M^2 = systematic variance; sigma_epsilon^2 = unsystematic (firm-specific) variance
formulas.use: Splits an asset's variance into priced systematic risk and diversifiable unsystematic risk.
formulas.trap: Writing beta x sigma_M^2 without squaring beta, or expecting a return premium for the unsystematic part.

formulas.name: Single-index market model
formulas.vars: alpha_i, beta_i = regression intercept and slope; e_i = firm-specific error with mean zero
formulas.use: Return-generating model: regress an asset's returns on market returns to estimate its beta.
formulas.trap: Reading the regression intercept as Jensen's alpha; the market model uses raw returns, not returns in excess of R_f.

formulas.name: Security characteristic line (SCL)
formulas.vars: Regression of the asset's excess return on the market's excess return; slope = beta_i, intercept = alpha_i
formulas.use: Plots an asset's excess return against the market's excess return; the slope estimates beta and the intercept is alpha.
formulas.trap: Confusing the SCL with the SML: the SCL is one asset's regression line over time; the SML prices all assets by beta.

formulas.name: Multifactor model expected return
formulas.vars: beta_i,k = sensitivity of asset i to factor k; E(F_k) = expected risk premium of factor k (e.g., market, SMB, HML)
formulas.use: Builds an expected excess return from several systematic factors, such as the Fama-French size and value factors.
formulas.trap: Confusing the sensitivity with the factor premium; each term multiplies a beta by a factor premium, they are not added.

formulas.name: Beta
formulas.use: Measures an asset's systematic risk relative to the market; the input to CAPM, Treynor and Jensen's alpha.
formulas.trap: Dividing covariance by sigma_M instead of sigma_M squared, or equating high total volatility with high beta.

formulas.name: Portfolio beta
formulas.use: Gives a portfolio's systematic risk as the weighted average of its holdings' betas.
formulas.trap: Expecting diversification to lower beta the way it lowers sigma; beta is a pure weighted average with no correlation effect.

formulas.name: CAPM required return
formulas.use: Required return on any asset or portfolio from its systematic risk; plotted against beta it is the SML.
formulas.trap: Multiplying beta by E(R_M) instead of the market risk premium E(R_M) - R_f, or adding a firm-specific risk premium.

formulas.name: Security market line alpha (forecast)
formulas.use: Positive alpha: forecast return above the SML, stock undervalued (buy); negative: below the SML, overvalued.
formulas.trap: Ranking stocks on forecast returns without adjusting for beta, or judging single stocks against the CML.

formulas.name: Sharpe ratio
formulas.use: Excess return per unit of total risk; ranks portfolios that make up the investor's entire holdings.
formulas.trap: Putting beta in the denominator (that is Treynor), or using Sharpe to rank a sleeve held inside a diversified portfolio.

formulas.name: Treynor ratio
formulas.use: Excess return per unit of systematic risk; ranks well-diversified portfolios or sleeves of a larger portfolio.
formulas.trap: Applying Treynor to an undiversified portfolio; beta ignores its large unsystematic risk, so it looks better than it is.

formulas.name: M-squared (M2)
formulas.vars: Some texts report the risk-adjusted return (R_p - R_f)(sigma_M / sigma_p) + R_f and compare it with R_M; the gap is the same
formulas.use: Expresses Sharpe-based outperformance in percent: the portfolio levered or delevered to market sigma, minus the market.
formulas.trap: Treating M-squared as beta-based like Jensen's alpha; it uses total risk and ranks portfolios exactly as Sharpe does.

formulas.name: Jensen's alpha
formulas.use: Realized return above the CAPM required return for the portfolio's beta; positive alpha means outperformance.
formulas.trap: Using total risk instead of beta in the required return, or comparing raw returns of managers with different betas.

definitions.def: Planning (IPS and capital market expectations), execution (asset allocation, security selection, portfolio construction) and feedback (monitoring, rebalancing, performance evaluation), repeated continuously.

definitions.term: Open-end vs closed-end funds vs ETFs
definitions.def: Open-end funds issue and redeem shares at NAV; closed-end funds have fixed shares that can trade at premiums or discounts to NAV; ETFs trade intraday and stay near NAV through in-kind creation and redemption.
The part of the minimum-variance frontier above the global minimum-variance portfolio: the highest expected return for each level of risk. Portfolios below that point are inefficient.
With a risk-free asset, the tangency portfolio where the CAL touches the efficient frontier and the Sharpe ratio is highest. Investors then pick their risk-free mix on that CAL by risk aversion.
Systematic (market) risk cannot be diversified away and is priced by beta. Unsystematic (firm-specific) risk can be diversified away at no cost, so investors earn no premium for bearing it.
The CML plots expected return against total risk for efficient portfolios only. The SML plots required return against beta for every asset, so mispricing of single stocks is judged on the SML.
States return and risk objectives plus constraints: liquidity, time horizon, taxes, legal and regulatory factors and unique circumstances, along with benchmarks, review and rebalancing policy.

definitions.term: Ability vs willingness to take risk
definitions.def: Ability depends on objective factors (horizon, wealth versus needs, income stability); willingness is psychological. When they conflict, generally adopt the lower of the two and educate the client.
Strategic allocation is the long-term policy mix set from the IPS and capital market expectations. Tactical allocation is a deliberate short-term deviation from it to exploit perceived mispricing.

Cognitive errors (conservatism, confirmation, anchoring, mental accounting) come from faulty reasoning and are usually moderated. Emotional biases (loss aversion, status quo, endowment) are often adapted to.
Feeling losses about twice as strongly as equal gains. It drives the disposition effect: selling winners too early and holding losers too long. It is an emotional bias, not a reasoning error.
Risk tolerance is how much risk the organization is willing to accept; risk budgeting allocates that total risk across activities or managers. The aim is to take the right risks, not the least.

VaR is the minimum loss expected with a given probability over a set horizon (5% one-month VaR), not the maximum loss. Conditional VaR (expected shortfall) is the average loss beyond the VaR threshold.
Risk transfer passes a risk to another party, typically through insurance. Risk shifting changes the distribution of outcomes, typically with derivatives such as forwards or options.

drill.why: Expected return penalized by half of risk aversion times variance is utility. Sharpe also trades return against risk but divides excess return by sigma; Jensen's alpha subtracts a CAPM return, not a variance.

Squared weights times variances plus the doubled cross term is two-asset portfolio variance. Total risk decomposition also sums two variance terms, but they are beta squared times market variance and residual variance.

Covariance with the market over market variance, or rho times the volatility ratio, is an asset's beta. Covariance from correlation multiplies both sigmas instead of dividing; portfolio beta is a weighted sum.
A line in total risk sigma_p whose slope is the market portfolio's Sharpe ratio is the CML. A CAL has the same shape for any risky portfolio i; CAPM uses beta, not sigma, on the x-axis.

Risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium is the CAPM required return. The CML scales the premium by sigma_p / sigma_M instead of beta; Jensen's alpha subtracts this CAPM return from R_p.

Excess return over the risk-free rate divided by total risk sigma_p is the Sharpe ratio. Treynor has the same numerator over beta; the CML uses the market's Sharpe ratio as a slope, not as the result.

Excess return per unit of beta is the Treynor ratio, a systematic-risk measure. Sharpe divides the same excess return by total risk sigma; Jensen's alpha uses beta but subtracts, giving a percent, not a ratio.

Scaling excess return to market sigma and subtracting the market premium gives M-squared, a percent version of Sharpe. Jensen's alpha is also a percent difference but adjusts for beta, not total risk.
Realized portfolio return minus its CAPM required return is Jensen's alpha, an ex post measure. SML alpha has the same shape but uses a forecast return to judge whether a stock is mispriced ex ante.
A regression of the asset's excess return on the market's excess return, with intercept and error, is the SCL. The market model regresses raw returns; CAPM has no intercept or error term.

code: Act with integrity, competence, diligence, respect, and ethically toward the public, clients, prospects, employers, employees, colleagues, and other market participants.
Place the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above your own personal interests.
Use reasonable care and exercise independent professional judgment in investment analysis, recommendations, actions, and other professional activities.
Practice, and encourage others to practice, in a professional and ethical manner that reflects credit on yourself and the profession.
Promote the integrity and viability of the global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society.
Maintain and improve your professional competence, and strive to maintain and improve the competence of other investment professionals.

standards.name: Knowledge of the Law
standards.requires: Know and follow the stricter of applicable law and the Code and Standards. Do not knowingly join or assist a violation: dissociate by going to your supervisor or compliance, refusing the work, and in extreme cases resigning.
standards.trap: Thinking the Standards require reporting violations to regulators (encouraged, not required), or that local law governs even when it is less strict than the Standards.

standards.name: Independence and Objectivity
standards.requires: Use reasonable care to stay independent and objective. Refuse issuer gifts beyond modest value, pay your own commercial travel to issuers (issuer travel only when none exists), and take issuer-paid research only for a flat fee.
standards.trap: Thinking a client's gift needs no disclosure to the employer, or that disclosing an investment banking tie cures a rating changed under deal pressure.

standards.name: Misrepresentation
standards.requires: Make no knowing misrepresentation about analysis, recommendations, actions, performance, services, or credentials. Credit others' opinions and work product even when paraphrased, and never guarantee returns on risky investments.
standards.trap: Assuming any public source may be used uncredited; only factual data from recognized statistical sources, such as a central bank, may be used without acknowledgment.

standards.name: Misconduct
standards.requires: Do not engage in professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit, or commit any act that reflects adversely on your professional reputation, integrity, or competence, such as padding expense reports.
standards.trap: Treating personal bankruptcy or a one-off off-duty incident as misconduct by itself; I(D) targets dishonesty, fraud, and acts that undermine professional integrity.

standards.name: Material Nonpublic Information
standards.requires: If you possess material nonpublic information, do not act or cause others to act on it. Urge the issuer to disclose it publicly, inform compliance, and trade only after the information has been disseminated.
standards.trap: Using mosaic theory to cover a material leak: it permits public plus nonmaterial nonpublic pieces only. The ban covers personal and client trades alike.

standards.name: Market Manipulation
standards.requires: Do not distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with intent to mislead market participants, whether transaction-based (wash trades, marking the close) or information-based (spreading false rumors).
standards.trap: Calling every price-moving trade manipulation: tax-loss selling and splitting a large order to cut market impact are legitimate. Intent to mislead is the test.

standards.name: Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
standards.requires: Act with loyalty, prudence, and care for clients' benefit, ahead of employer and self. Identify the true client (plan beneficiaries, not the sponsor), vote material proxies, and seek best execution.
standards.trap: Treating soft dollars as the firm's money: commissions belong to the client and may buy only research that assists that client's investment decisions.

standards.name: Fair Dealing
standards.requires: Deal fairly and objectively with all clients when disseminating recommendations, changing them, or taking action. Send changes to all clients near-simultaneously and allocate oversubscribed issues pro rata by a disclosed method.
standards.trap: Confusing fair with equal: disclosed premium service tiers are allowed, but no client group may get a time advantage on a new or changed recommendation.

standards.name: Suitability
standards.requires: Learn each client's objectives and constraints, write an IPS and review it at least annually and after major life events, and judge suitability for the total portfolio. For pooled funds, manage to the stated mandate.
standards.trap: Judging suitability security by security, or refusing every unsolicited trade; a small one may proceed after explaining risks and documenting who initiated it.

standards.name: Performance Presentation
standards.requires: Make reasonable efforts to keep performance information fair, accurate, and complete: include terminated accounts, state gross or net of fees, label simulated results, and offer full details behind any brief presentation.
standards.trap: Believing III(D) requires GIPS compliance. It does not, but cherry-picked or survivorship-biased results breach it even when labeled representative.

standards.name: Preservation of Confidentiality
standards.requires: Keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless it concerns illegal client activity, disclosure is required by law, or the client permits it. Helping the Professional Conduct Program is allowed.
standards.trap: Thinking confidentiality ends when the account closes, or that it is absolute and bars reporting suspected money laundering that local law requires you to report.

standards.name: Loyalty
standards.requires: Act for your employer's benefit and do not harm it. You may prepare to leave, but do not solicit clients or take client lists, models, or records before departure. Get consent before starting competing independent practice.
standards.trap: Thinking all preparation to compete is disloyal, or that loyalty means hiding employer misconduct; whistleblowing to protect clients or markets is permitted.

standards.name: Additional Compensation Arrangements
standards.requires: Do not accept gifts, benefits, or compensation that compete with or might conflict with your employer's interest unless you first obtain written consent from all parties involved, disclosing terms, amount, and duration.
standards.trap: Treating a client's bonus for future performance as an ordinary I(B) gift, or relying on verbal approval or on telling the employer after the money arrives.

standards.name: Responsibilities of Supervisors
standards.requires: Make reasonable efforts to ensure supervisees follow laws, rules, and the Code and Standards. Investigate suspected breaches promptly and limit their activity. If compliance systems are inadequate, decline in writing to supervise.
standards.trap: Believing delegation transfers the supervisory duty, or that a written compliance manual is enough when nobody checks that it is actually applied.

standards.name: Diligence and Reasonable Basis
standards.requires: Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness, and have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by research, for every recommendation. Assess third-party research, understand quantitative models, and vet external managers.
standards.trap: Thinking you must dissociate from every group report you disagree with; if the consensus had a reasonable basis, document your dissent and stay on it.

standards.name: Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
standards.requires: Disclose the basic format and general principles of the investment process, its significant risks and limitations, and any material change to it promptly. Distinguish fact from opinion in analysis and recommendations.
standards.trap: Presenting an EPS or price forecast as fact, or delaying notice of a process change, such as adding leverage, until the annual report.

standards.name: Record Retention
standards.requires: Develop and keep records that support investment analysis, recommendations, actions, and client communications. Records belong to the employer; absent a regulatory period, CFA Institute recommends at least seven years.
standards.trap: Assuming the analyst owns her research and may take it to a new firm; she must recreate it from public sources or the covered company.

standards.name: Disclosure of Conflicts
standards.requires: Make full, fair, and prominent disclosure to your employer, clients, and prospects of every matter that could reasonably impair independence and objectivity, including beneficial ownership, family ties, and board seats.
standards.trap: Disclosing only to compliance or in fine print, or thinking only direct share ownership counts; a spouse's holding or job at the issuer must be disclosed.

standards.name: Priority of Transactions
standards.requires: Client and employer transactions take priority over trades in which you are a beneficial owner: clients first, then employer, then self. A family member's fee-paying account is treated like any other client account.
standards.trap: Disadvantaging a family member's client account to avoid looking biased, or buying a hot IPO personally while clients are underfilled because the price is the same.

standards.name: Referral Fees
standards.requires: Disclose to your employer, clients, and prospects, before the engagement begins, any compensation or benefit received from or paid to others for recommending products or services, with its nature and estimated value.
standards.trap: Disclosing the referral fee only to the employer, or telling the client only after they have already signed with the referred provider.

standards.name: Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
standards.requires: Do not compromise the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute, the CFA designation, or its exams: no cheating, no disclosing questions, topics, or formulas tested, and no misrepresenting information to CFA Institute.
standards.trap: Thinking exam content may be shared once the exam is over, or that publicly criticizing CFA Institute policy is a violation; general impressions are fine.

standards.name: Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
standards.requires: Do not misrepresent or exaggerate CFA membership, the designation, or candidacy. Use CFA as an adjective, keep membership current (dues plus the annual conduct statement), and never imply a partial designation.
standards.trap: Writing 'CFA Level II' or 'a CFA', or claiming the charter produces superior returns; write 'Level II candidate in the CFA Program' instead.

definitions.def: Law sets the minimum and often lags market practice; ethical conduct can demand more. Not illegal does not mean ethical, and where law is silent the Code and Standards still apply.

Identify facts, stakeholders, duties, and conflicts; consider situational influences such as bonuses and firm culture and seek guidance; decide and act; then reflect. It is iterative, not a legality check.
Information a reasonable investor would consider important in deciding to trade, or that would likely move the price if disclosed. Specific, reliable information is more likely to be material.
Information not yet disseminated to the market at large. Telling a few analysts on a private call does not make it public; a press release or regulatory filing does.
Reaching a material conclusion by combining public information with nonmaterial nonpublic pieces is permitted. It fails if any single piece is material and nonpublic. Keep records of the mosaic.
A watch list is a confidential compliance list of issuers where the firm holds MNPI, used to monitor trading. A restricted list openly bars trading and recommendations in the name.

Procedures that stop MNPI and deal pressure flowing from investment banking to research and trading: compliance-controlled contact, separate reporting lines, and analyst pay not tied to banking deals.
Research or services paid for with client brokerage commissions. Commissions belong to the client, so they may buy only research that assists that client's decisions; mixed-use items are split.
Filling every client order for an oversubscribed issue in proportion to its size, under a method disclosed in advance. Employee and personal accounts participate only after clients are filled.
Voluntary global standards for calculating and presenting investment performance based on fair representation and full disclosure, so prospects can compare managers' track records directly.

Only an investment firm (or an asset owner) can claim compliance, and only firm-wide; a fund, strategy, composite, or software vendor cannot. Compliance is voluntary, but a claim means meeting every requirement.
An investment firm, subsidiary, or division held out to clients as a distinct business entity. It sets the boundary for total firm assets and for which portfolios must be placed in composites.
A group of portfolios managed to a similar mandate, objective, or strategy, defined in advance. All actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios must be in at least one composite.

A portfolio the manager can run to the intended strategy. Mild client restrictions, such as an energy exclusion, keep it discretionary; restrictions that block the strategy, such as approving every trade, do not.

Independent third-party testing, firm-wide, of composite construction and of the policies for calculating and presenting performance. Recommended, not required; it does not certify any one composite's returns.
A firm either meets every applicable GIPS requirement and uses the required compliance statement or makes no claim. Phrases such as 'consistent with GIPS' or 'GIPS except for fees' are prohibited.
